title: Your first course-grounded feed
scope: Expanding, uncapped coverage of current assignments and lecture concepts, with supporting textbook sections. Includes concept explanations, calculation prompts, derivation steps, implementation pitfalls, and cross-course connections. Coverage is tracked in coverage.json; card presence is not proof of mastery or exhaustive source review.

cards.title: The number after 99 is not 100.
cards.body:
In IEEE binary64, what is the next representable number larger than 99?

Start by finding the power-of-two interval containing 99.
cards.answer:
99 lies in [2⁶, 2⁷). Binary64 has 53 significant binary digits, so spacing in this interval is 2⁽⁶⁻⁵²⁾ = 2⁻⁴⁶. The next number is 99 + 2⁻⁴⁶.

Spacing is constant inside a power-of-two interval, then doubles at the next boundary.
cards.takeaway: Spacing depends on magnitude.

cards.title: A uniform draw becomes a waiting time.
cards.body: Let U be uniform on (0,1). Find a transformation of U that produces an exponential waiting time with rate λ > 0.
cards.answer:
The exponential CDF is F(t) = 1 − e⁻ˡᵗ. Solving U = F(t) gives T = −log(1 − U)/λ. Since 1 − U is also uniform, −log(U)/λ has the same distribution.

Keep the logarithm input strictly positive. The mean waiting time is 1/λ.
cards.takeaway: Invert the CDF to change the distribution.

cards.title: A model is a space of possible means.
cards.body: For an n × p matrix X, why is {Xβ : β ∈ ℝᵖ} a subspace of ℝⁿ?
cards.answer:
It contains zero because X0 = 0. It is closed under addition because Xβ₁ + Xβ₂ = X(β₁ + β₂). It is closed under scalar multiplication because cXβ = X(cβ).

This column space is the set of mean vectors the linear model can represent.
cards.takeaway: The columns define the model’s possibilities.

cards.title: The two gaps beside 2 are different.
cards.body: What are the binary64 gaps immediately below and immediately above 2?
cards.answer: Below 2, numbers lie in [1,2) and the gap is 2⁻⁵². Above 2, they lie in [2,4) and the gap is 2⁻⁵¹. The next larger number is 2 + 2⁻⁵¹, while the predecessor is 2 − 2⁻⁵².
cards.takeaway: Spacing changes at a power-of-two boundary.

cards.title: Why does inverting the CDF work?
cards.body: Assume F is continuous and strictly increasing and U is uniform on (0,1). Show that X=F⁻¹(U) has CDF F.
cards.answer: P(X≤x)=P(F⁻¹(U)≤x)=P(U≤F(x))=F(x). Monotonicity lets you move the inequality through F. A generalized inverse extends the method to distributions with jumps or flat regions.
cards.takeaway: Prove the distribution through its CDF.

cards.title: Which space does each vector live in?
cards.body: For an n×p design matrix X, identify the ambient spaces of β, Xβ, C(X), and N(X).
cards.answer: β and N(X) live in ℝᵖ, the coefficient space. Xβ and C(X) live in ℝⁿ, the observation space. Confusing these spaces makes expressions like “the residual lies in N(X)” dimensionally wrong; ordinary least-squares residuals lie in N(Xᵀ).
cards.takeaway: Check dimensions before proving a statement.

cards.title: Two constants often share the name epsilon.
cards.body: In binary64 with round-to-nearest, distinguish the gap between 1 and its successor from the usual unit roundoff u.
cards.answer: The gap is 2⁻⁵². Unit roundoff is u = 2⁻⁵³, half that spacing, used in the relative rounding bound for normal results. Some software calls the former machine epsilon; some texts use epsilon for the latter. Check the convention before applying an error bound.
cards.takeaway: State the convention, not just the symbol.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Move a uniform draw into a new interval.
cards.body: Given U∼Uniform(0,1), create a draw uniform on [−2,5]. What is its density?
cards.answer: X=−2+7U is uniform on that interval. Its density is 1/7 there and zero outside. A translation sets the lower endpoint; scaling sets the interval length.
cards.takeaway: Shift and scale the unit interval.

sources.locator: Linear algebra notes · subspaces and rank

cards.title: Count identifiable and invisible directions.
cards.body: X is a 10×4 matrix of rank 3. What are dim C(X), dim N(X), and dim C(X)⊥?
cards.answer: They are 3, 4−3=1, and 10−3=7. One coefficient-space direction is invisible to the mean, while seven observation-space directions are perpendicular to the fitted-value space. These dimensions refer to two different ambient spaces.
cards.takeaway: Rank-nullity depends on the domain dimension.
cards.source: Linear algebra notes · subspaces and rank · companion practice

cards.title: Build a tiny floating-point grid.
cards.body: A normalized binary system has p=3 significant bits, including the leading 1. List its representable values in [1,2).
cards.answer: The significands are 1.00₂, 1.01₂, 1.10₂, and 1.11₂. They represent 1, 1.25, 1.5, and 1.75. The gap is 2^(1−p)=1/4. In [2,4), multiply these values by 2, so the gap becomes 1/2.
cards.takeaway: Build one interval, then scale it.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Rate and scale are reciprocals.
cards.body: For an exponential rate λ=4 per second, what are the mean and variance of a waiting time?
cards.answer: Mean is 1/λ=0.25 seconds. Variance is 1/λ²=1/16 second². A random-number API using an exponential scale parameter expects 0.25, not 4. Check parameter conventions before sampling.
cards.takeaway: Rate has inverse-time units; scale has time units.

cards.title: The model can stay fixed even if every column changes.
cards.body: If two design matrices have different columns, must they define different least-squares mean models?
cards.answer: No. Different bases can span the same column space. The model consists of all possible Xβ vectors, not the particular list of columns. Compare column spaces and constraints, not just the literal entries.
cards.takeaway: A basis is a representation of a space.

cards.title: When does adding one stop moving?
cards.body: Binary64 represents every integer up to 2⁵³ exactly. What happens to 2⁵³ + 1 in round-to-nearest, ties-to-even arithmetic?
cards.answer: In [2⁵³,2⁵⁴), adjacent numbers are spaced by 2. The exact result lies halfway between 2⁵³ and 2⁵³+2, and the tie rule selects 2⁵³. This does not mean all integers above 2⁵³ are unrepresentable: the even ones in this interval are representable.
cards.takeaway: Exact integers stop being consecutive.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Survival for another interval forgets the elapsed wait.
cards.body: For T∼Exp(λ), compute P(T>s+t | T>s).
cards.answer: It is P(T>s+t)/P(T>s)=exp(−λ(s+t))/exp(−λs)=exp(−λt). The conditional remaining waiting time has the original distribution. This property applies to a constant hazard, not to arbitrary waiting-time laws.
cards.takeaway: Exponential survival makes the elapsed time cancel.

cards.title: Which direction can neither column reach?
cards.body:
X has columns (1,1,0)ᵀ and (0,1,1)ᵀ.

Find all vectors perpendicular to both columns.
cards.answer:
For v = (a,b,c)ᵀ, orthogonality requires a + b = 0 and b + c = 0. Thus v = t(1,−1,1)ᵀ.

In general, C(X)⊥ = N(Xᵀ). Be careful about orientation: N(X) instead equals C(Xᵀ)⊥.
cards.takeaway: Orthogonality becomes a null-space equation.

cards.title: Gradual underflow trades relative precision for range.
cards.body: What happens to floating-point spacing in the subnormal range?
cards.answer: Subnormals use a fixed minimum exponent and allow a leading zero significand. Their absolute spacing is constant, extending values toward zero. Relative spacing grows as the values shrink, so the usual small relative-error bound for normal values no longer applies uniformly.
cards.takeaway: Subnormals preserve small absolute values.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Ten times more precise costs how much?
cards.body:
For independent samples with finite variance, a Monte Carlo average has standard error σ/√N.

How many samples do you need to shrink that error by a factor of 10?
cards.answer:
100 times as many. Solving σ/√N_new = (σ/√N_old)/10 gives N_new = 100 N_old.

The N⁻¹ᐟ² exponent is dimension-independent, but variance, evaluation cost, and relative error can still depend strongly on dimension.
cards.takeaway: Error shrinks with √N, not N.

cards.title: Orthogonal to every row means annihilated by X.
cards.body: Prove N(X)=C(Xᵀ)⊥ by looking at row-vector dot products.
cards.answer: Xv=0 means every row of X has dot product zero with v. Therefore v is orthogonal to every linear combination of those rows, which form C(Xᵀ). Conversely, orthogonality to the row space includes each row, so every component of Xv is zero.
cards.takeaway: A null-space equation is a collection of orthogonality tests.

cards.title: Count the gaps. Then count the endpoints.
cards.body:
How many binary64 numbers lie in the closed interval [1.5, 2]?

The spacing below 2 is 2⁻⁵².
cards.answer:
There are (2 − 1.5) / 2⁻⁵² = 2⁵¹ gaps. Both endpoints are representable and included, so there are 2⁵¹ + 1 numbers.

The larger spacing above 2 does not change the number of points up to and including 2.
cards.takeaway: Numbers = gaps + 1.

cards.title: An integral is an average times volume.
cards.body: To estimate ∫₂⁵f(x)dx using independent uniform samples on [2,5], what estimator do you use?
cards.answer: Use 3·N⁻¹Σf(Xᵢ). Uniform density is 1/3, so the sample average estimates one third of the integral. On a d-dimensional region sampled uniformly, multiply by the region’s volume.
cards.takeaway: Do not forget the domain-volume factor.

cards.title: Split a vector into its mean and centered part.
cards.body: For y=(1,2,6)ᵀ, project onto span((1,1,1)ᵀ), then compute the orthogonal residual.
cards.answer: The projection is the mean times the ones vector: (3,3,3)ᵀ. The residual is (−2,−1,3)ᵀ. Its components sum to zero, so it is perpendicular to the ones vector. Their sum recovers y.
cards.takeaway: Centering removes the intercept-space component.

cards.title: A nonrepresentable endpoint does not get an extra point.
cards.body: For a uniform grid a+kδ, k≥0, count grid points in [a,b] when b need not lie on the grid.
cards.answer: The largest allowed k is floor((b−a)/δ). Including k=0 gives floor((b−a)/δ)+1 points. Do not round the quotient to the nearest integer. For the homework interval [1/2,2/3], δ=2⁻⁵³, giving floor(2⁵³/6)+1.
cards.takeaway: Use a floor when the upper endpoint is between points.

cards.title: Linearity of expectation proves unbiasedness.
cards.body: For identically distributed draws with E[f(Xᵢ)]=I, why is Î=N⁻¹Σf(Xᵢ) unbiased? Is independence required for that step?
cards.answer: E[Î]=N⁻¹ΣE[f(Xᵢ)]=I. Independence is not required for this expectation identity. Independence matters for the simple variance formula σ²/N; dependence adds covariance terms.
cards.takeaway: Separate the unbiasedness argument from the variance argument.
cards.source: HW1 · Q2 · Monte Carlo integration · companion practice

cards.title: Unidentified coefficients can still give an identified answer.
cards.body: Suppose β is not unique because X has dependent columns. What condition makes ℓᵀβ estimable by a linear unbiased estimator?
cards.answer:
There must be an a with Xᵀa = ℓ, meaning ℓ lies in C(Xᵀ), the row space of X. Then E[aᵀy] = aᵀXβ = ℓᵀβ.

Equivalently, ℓ must be orthogonal to every null direction of X, so changing β without changing Xβ cannot change the target ℓᵀβ.
cards.takeaway: Estimate what the data can distinguish.

cards.title: Different inputs. The same reciprocal.
cards.body: Real-number reciprocals are one-to-one. Why can two different floating-point inputs produce exactly the same computed reciprocal?
cards.answer: Rounding maps a continuum of exact results onto a finite grid. For inputs in [1.5, 2], exact reciprocals lie in [0.5, 2/3]. That output interval contains fewer binary64 grid points than the input interval. In binary64, rounding 2/3 goes downward, so rounded outputs remain in this interval. By the pigeonhole principle, at least two inputs share an output.
cards.takeaway: Rounding can destroy one-to-one mappings.

cards.title: Estimate the sampling error, not the spread of individual draws.
cards.body: Function values have sample standard deviation s=3 across N=900 independent draws. Estimate the standard error of their mean.
cards.answer: s/√N=3/30=0.1. The value 3 describes variation of individual function evaluations; 0.1 describes estimated variation of the average across repeated samples. If estimating an integral with a volume factor, multiply the standard error by that factor too.
cards.takeaway: Spread of draws and uncertainty of their average differ.
cards.source: HW1 · Q2 · Monte Carlo integration · companion practice

cards.title: A sum can be estimable when its pieces are not.
cards.body: Suppose X=[x x] with x≠0. Are β₁, β₂, β₁+β₂, and β₁−β₂ identifiable from the mean?
cards.answer: The mean is x(β₁+β₂), so only the sum among these targets is identifiable. Adding t to β₁ and subtracting t from β₂ leaves the mean unchanged but changes either individual coefficient and their difference. The row space is span((1,1)ᵀ).
cards.takeaway: Look for functions unchanged by null directions.

cards.title: A collision must exist. That does not locate it.
cards.body: A counting argument proves that some floating-point reciprocals collide. Does it imply every pair of adjacent inputs has equal reciprocals?
cards.answer: No. More inputs than possible rounded outputs guarantees at least one collision, not a collision at each adjacent pair. To locate examples, evaluate neighboring machine numbers, for example with nextafter. The proof and the search answer different questions.
cards.takeaway: Existence is not a statement about every pair.

cards.title: RMSE equals standard deviation only when bias is zero.
cards.body: State the decomposition of mean squared estimation error into variance and squared bias.
cards.answer: E[(Î−I)²]=Var(Î)+(E[Î]−I)². For an unbiased estimator, RMSE=√Var(Î). For a biased estimator, a reported standard error does not account for the squared-bias contribution.
cards.takeaway: Error bars about a mean do not automatically include bias.
cards.source: HW1 · Q2 · Monte Carlo integration · companion practice

cards.title: Estimability tells you how to build an estimator.
cards.body: If ℓ=Xᵀa and E[y]=Xβ, why is aᵀy an unbiased estimator of ℓᵀβ?
cards.answer: E[aᵀy]=aᵀE[y]=aᵀXβ=(Xᵀa)ᵀβ=ℓᵀβ. This is why membership in the row space is sufficient. Conversely, any linear estimator unbiased for all β must satisfy this coefficient identity.
cards.takeaway: Match the expectation coefficient-by-coefficient.

cards.title: “Multiplying by the reciprocal always gives one.”
cards.body:
A programmer asserts k * (1.0 / k) == 1.0 for every positive integer k representable in binary64.

Why is this guaranteed for k = 4, but not by the same reasoning for k = 5?
cards.answer: 1/4 = 2⁻² is exactly representable, and multiplying by 4 gives exactly 1. In contrast, 1/5 has a repeating binary expansion and is rounded. The subsequent multiplication is rounded again. It may still produce exactly 1, but the real-arithmetic identity alone does not guarantee it.
cards.takeaway: An algebraic identity is not a rounding guarantee.

cards.title: The grid pays for every dimension.
cards.body:
A smooth integrand gives composite midpoint error O(h²). A d-dimensional tensor grid uses N points.

What is its error rate in N, and when does its exponent match Monte Carlo?
cards.answer:
Since N is proportional to h⁻ᵈ, h is proportional to N⁻¹ᐟᵈ. Midpoint error is therefore O(N⁻²ᐟᵈ). This matches the Monte Carlo N⁻¹ᐟ² exponent at d = 4.

These are rates under the stated smoothness and finite-variance assumptions; constants still matter for a finite computation.
cards.takeaway: A grid costs nᵈ points.

cards.title: A group difference survives an arbitrary baseline shift.
cards.body: In μᵢ=α+γᵢ with all γ levels unconstrained, is γ₂−γ₁ identifiable even though α and individual γᵢ are not?
cards.answer: Yes, when those group means are represented in the observed design: γ₂−γ₁=μ₂−μ₁. A shift α→α+c and γᵢ→γᵢ−c cancels in the difference. Identifiability of a contrast does not require identifying every coefficient separately.
cards.takeaway: Differences can remove the redundant baseline.

cards.title: Why does 0.5 terminate but 0.1 repeat?
cards.body: What property of a reduced rational fraction determines whether it has a terminating binary expansion?
cards.answer: Its denominator must be a power of 2. Multiplying by enough powers of 2 must turn it into an integer. The denominator of 1/2 meets this condition; the reduced denominator of 1/10 includes a factor of 5, so its binary expansion repeats.
cards.takeaway: The denominator determines which base can terminate.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: A million points can still mean a coarse high-dimensional grid.
cards.body: With N=nᵈ≤10⁶ and d=8, what is the largest integer n allowed per axis?
cards.answer: n≤(10⁶)^(1/8)≈5.623, so n=5. The grid uses 5⁸=390,625 points; n=6 would require 1,679,616. Large total counts can still give poor resolution along every coordinate.
cards.takeaway: Exponential growth in dimension consumes resolution.

cards.title: A new prediction can be unidentified.
cards.body: With rank-deficient training matrix X, when is a proposed mean prediction x₀β uniquely determined by the training mean model?
cards.answer: When the row vector x₀ lies in the row space of X. Equivalently, x₀v=0 for every v∈N(X). Otherwise two coefficient vectors producing identical training means can give different x₀β. A solver selecting one coefficient vector does not resolve that informational ambiguity.
cards.takeaway: A numerical choice does not make an estimand identifiable.

cards.title: Which side does the operation go on?
cards.body:
You want to double row 1 of B, then add column 3 to column 2.

Which operation multiplies B from the left, and which from the right?
cards.answer:
Row operations act from the left: LB. Column operations act from the right: BC. Together the result is LBC. For the column addition, C is the identity with an extra 1 at entry (3,2).

Order matters: later left operations appear farther left; later right operations appear farther right.
cards.takeaway: Rows: left. Columns: right.

cards.title: Factor the separable integral before approximating it.
cards.body: For f(x)=exp(−Σxᵢ²) on [0,1]ᵈ, why does the integral equal [∫₀¹exp(−u²)du]ᵈ?
cards.answer: The exponential factors into ∏exp(−xᵢ²), and the domain is a product of identical intervals. Repeated integration separates the factors. Each one-dimensional integral equals √π erf(1)/2. The analytic factorization provides a useful reference for the numerical methods.
cards.takeaway: Exploit separability when both function and domain allow it.

cards.title: One least-squares problem. Two different questions.
cards.body: You minimize ‖Xβ − y‖². What does each course ask about this same operation?
cards.answer:
AM 205: Can the numerical algorithm compute a reliable solution? QR avoids explicitly forming the normal equations, whose condition number squares that of a full-column-rank design.
STAT 244: What is the projection geometry, and under what assumptions do estimates support inference? A stable numerical answer alone does not establish those statistical assumptions.
cards.takeaway: Numerical reliability and valid inference require different checks.

cards.title: Swapping first is not the same as scaling first.
cards.body: Take B=[[1,2],[3,4]]. Scale row 1 by 2, then swap the rows. What result do you get? What if you reverse the steps?
cards.answer: Scale then swap gives [[3,4],[2,4]]. Swap then scale gives [[6,8],[1,2]]. If S scales row 1 and P swaps rows, the operations are PSB versus SPB. Matrix multiplication is generally noncommutative.
cards.takeaway: Later row operations multiply farther left.

cards.title: A slope of minus one-half predicts a concrete gain.
cards.body: An error curve behaves like E(N)=CN⁻¹ᐟ² on a log–log plot. What happens to error when N is multiplied by 16?
cards.answer: The error is multiplied by 16⁻¹ᐟ²=1/4. A fitted slope describes the scaling exponent, not the error constant C. Two methods can have different finite-budget performance even when one has a better asymptotic slope.
cards.takeaway: Read both slope and vertical position.

cards.title: One intercept. Every category. One dependency.
cards.body:
You include an intercept and an indicator column for every level of a categorical predictor.

What makes the coefficients nonidentifiable?
cards.answer:
The indicators sum to the intercept column. Adding c to the intercept and subtracting c from every category coefficient leaves every fitted value unchanged.

Drop one indicator, remove the intercept for a single-factor model, or impose an appropriate constraint. These choices can identify coefficients while preserving the same fitted-value space.
cards.takeaway: Different coefficients can encode the same model.

cards.title: Where does the off-diagonal one go?
cards.body: You want column 1 ← column 1 + 3 column 2 for an m×2 matrix B. Write the right multiplier.
cards.answer: Use C=[[1,0],[3,1]], so BC has first column B[:,1]+3B[:,2] in one-based notation and leaves the second unchanged. Each column of C supplies the coefficients for the corresponding output column.
cards.takeaway: Read a right multiplier one output column at a time.

cards.title: The normalizing constant disappears.
cards.body: You know a target density only up to a constant: π(x) = f(x)/Z. With a symmetric random-walk proposal, can you still run Metropolis–Hastings?
cards.answer:
Yes. The acceptance probability is min(1, π(x′)/π(x)) = min(1, f(x′)/f(x)); Z cancels. Symmetry also cancels the proposal ratio.

For a nonsymmetric proposal, retain q(x | x′)/q(x′ | x). Evaluate log ratios when densities are extremely small.
cards.takeaway: Ratios can be easier than normalized densities.

cards.title: Four columns can span only three directions.
cards.body: For one factor with three observed levels, your design has an intercept and three level indicators. What is its rank, assuming every level appears?
cards.answer: Rank 3, not 4. The intercept equals the sum of the indicator columns. The three indicators are independent when each level occurs, so they span a three-dimensional group-mean space. Drop one indicator with the intercept, or use all three without an intercept.
cards.takeaway: Count independent directions, not column labels.

cards.title: A circle goes into a matrix.
cards.body:
You sample points uniformly by area in a unit disk, then plot Ax for a nonsingular 2 × 2 matrix A.

What shape appears, and what controls its principal axis lengths?
cards.answer:
A filled ellipse. The singular values of A are the semiaxis lengths, and its left singular vectors give the principal axis directions. If A is singular, the image collapses to a line segment or a point.

Sampling radius uniformly is not uniform by area: use radius √U with U uniform on [0,1], or rejection sampling in the square.
cards.takeaway: Linear maps turn disks into ellipses.

cards.title: The reverse proposal probability matters.
cards.body: At current x and proposed y, π(y)/π(x)=2, q(x|y)=0.1, and q(y|x)=0.5. What is the MH acceptance probability?
cards.answer: α=min(1,2×0.1/0.5)=0.4. A higher target density does not guarantee acceptance for an asymmetric proposal: the proposal ratio compensates for directional bias.
cards.takeaway: Use target ratio times reverse-to-forward proposal ratio.

cards.title: An identifying constraint need not remove mean vectors.
cards.body: Why can setting one group effect to zero resolve coefficient ambiguity without restricting the possible group means?
cards.answer: The intercept can absorb that reference effect, and the remaining effects express differences from it. Every original set of group means still has a representation. This is a change of coordinates; a substantive restriction such as “all group means are equal” would shrink the model space.
cards.takeaway: Separate identifying conventions from scientific assumptions.

cards.title: Stretching two directions multiplies area.
cards.body: A 2×2 linear map has singular values 3 and 1/2. What happens to a unit disk’s semiaxes and area?
cards.answer: The semiaxes become 3 and 1/2. The area is π×3×1/2=3π/2. The area scale |det(A)| equals the product of singular values, 3/2; the determinant’s sign would additionally indicate orientation.
cards.takeaway: Singular values describe length; their product describes volume.

cards.title: Subtract log densities before exponentials underflow.
cards.body: For a symmetric proposal, write the log-space MH acceptance comparison using U∼Uniform(0,1).
cards.answer: Compute Δ=logπ(y)−logπ(x), then accept if log U<min(0,Δ). Comparing log U<Δ is equivalent because log U≤0. Avoid separately exponentiating very negative log densities and dividing two underflowed zeros.
cards.takeaway: Ratios become stable differences on the log scale.

cards.title: New coordinates. Same predictions.
cards.body: Let A be invertible. Why do ordinary least-squares models with design matrices X and XA have the same fitted values?
cards.answer:
Every XAγ equals Xβ with β = Aγ, and every Xβ equals XA(A⁻¹β). Their column spaces are identical. Both fitted vectors are the unique orthogonal projection of y onto that space.

Coefficients change coordinates. The fitted vector, residuals, and SSE do not.
cards.takeaway: Predictions depend on the space, not its basis.

cards.title: One nonzero singular value leaves a line segment.
cards.body: For A=[[2,0],[0,0]], what is the image of the unit disk? Is it a filled ellipse with positive area?
cards.answer: It is the segment {(x,0): −2≤x≤2}. The second coordinate is always zero, so the map has rank one and area zero. This is a degenerate ellipse, not a two-dimensional region.
cards.takeaway: Rank counts surviving directions.

cards.title: The accepted probability flow is a symmetric minimum.
cards.body: Show why MH’s accepted off-diagonal flow π(x)q(y|x)α(x,y) satisfies detailed balance.
cards.answer: Substitute α=min(1,π(y)q(x|y)/(π(x)q(y|x))). The flow becomes min(π(x)q(y|x),π(y)q(x|y)), unchanged when x and y are exchanged. The rejection probability supplies the remaining self-transition mass.
cards.takeaway: Detailed balance follows from the same two-way minimum.

cards.title: Which direction does the coefficient transformation go?
cards.body: If X*=XA with invertible A and Xβ=X*γ, how are β and γ related when X has full column rank?
cards.answer: β=Aγ and γ=A⁻¹β. Substitution gives XAγ=Xβ, and full column rank makes the coefficient representation unique. If X is rank deficient, Aγ−β may also lie in N(X); equality of mean vectors alone no longer forces coefficient equality.
cards.takeaway: Track the rank assumption when equating coefficients.
cards.source: HW2 · Q1 and Q4 · companion practice

cards.title: Rotations cannot change Euclidean length.
cards.body: If QᵀQ=I, show that ‖Qx‖₂=‖x‖₂. What does Q do to the unit disk when Q is square?
cards.answer: ‖Qx‖₂²=xᵀQᵀQx=xᵀx. A square orthogonal map preserves the unit disk, possibly rotating or reflecting it. All its singular values equal one.
cards.takeaway: Orthogonal coordinates preserve Euclidean geometry.

cards.title: Rejected does not mean deleted.
cards.body: A sampler saves only accepted proposals and discards every rejected step. Does this generally preserve the intended target distribution?
cards.answer: No. On a rejection, the next chain state equals the previous state, and that repeat counts as a sample. These holding times are part of the Markov transition kernel. Dropping repeats produces a jump chain that generally has a different stationary distribution.
cards.takeaway: A repeated state is still a sample.

cards.title: Equal full-rank spaces imply an invertible change of basis.
cards.body: X₁ and X₂ are n×p, both full column rank, with equal column spaces. Why can X₁=X₂A only use a nonsingular A?
cards.answer: Each column of X₁ lies in C(X₂), so its coordinates give a column of A. If A were singular, some nonzero v would satisfy Av=0. Then X₁v=X₂Av=0, contradicting full column rank of X₁.
cards.takeaway: Coordinate changes between bases are invertible.
cards.source: HW2 · Q1 and Q4 · companion practice

cards.title: A tiny pivot can make a big mess.
cards.body:
The first pivot is 10⁻¹², while entries below it are 5 and 13.

Why can elimination without pivoting lose accuracy even when the matrix is nonsingular?
cards.answer:
The multipliers become 5 × 10¹² and 13 × 10¹². Intermediate entries grow huge; later subtractions can leave small results whose relative rounding error is large. Partial pivoting chooses the largest magnitude entry in the active column, avoiding this tiny first pivot.

Nonsingularity guarantees an exact solution, not an accurate implementation.
cards.takeaway: Algorithmic stability is a separate question.

cards.title: Discarding self-transitions can erase a 90–10 balance.
cards.body: A two-state chain has P(A→B)=0.1 and P(B→A)=0.9. Its stationary probabilities are (0.9,0.1). What happens if you retain only state changes?
cards.answer: The retained sequence alternates A,B,A,B,…, so its long-run frequencies are 1/2 and 1/2. The original chain spends longer holding at A. Dropping repeated states removes those residence times and changes the distribution represented by the stored sequence.
cards.takeaway: Holding times carry stationary weight.

cards.title: All solutions form a shifted null space.
cards.body: If β̂ is one least-squares solution, what are all the others? When is the solution set itself a vector space?
cards.answer:
All solutions are β̂ + N(X): adding a null vector leaves the fitted values unchanged. This is an affine space.

It is a vector subspace exactly when it contains zero, equivalently when β̂ ∈ N(X), or Xβ̂ = 0. Otherwise the shift takes it away from the origin.
cards.takeaway: An affine space need not contain zero.

cards.title: A zero first pivot does not prove singularity.
cards.body: Consider A=[[0,1],[1,0]]. Can elimination without row exchanges begin? Is A singular?
cards.answer: The first pivot is zero, so standard unpivoted elimination cannot divide by it. But det(A)=−1, and swapping the rows gives the identity. The matrix is nonsingular and perfectly conditioned in the 2-norm. Pivoting is needed even for some well-conditioned matrices.
cards.takeaway: Algorithmic breakdown is not the same as singularity.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: From uniform to heavy-tailed.
cards.body:
What transformation of U ∼ Uniform(0,1) gives a Cauchy proposal centered at x with scale γ?

Does this random-walk proposal require a nontrivial proposal ratio in MH?
cards.answer:
Use x′ = x + γ tan(π(U − 1/2)). The Cauchy CDF is 1/2 + arctan((x′ − x)/γ)/π. Inverting it gives that transformation.

With fixed γ the proposal is symmetric about x, so q(x′ | x) = q(x | x′); the proposal ratio cancels.
cards.takeaway: Heavy tails from the tangent transform.

cards.title: Draw all least-squares coefficients for duplicate columns.
cards.body: If X=[x x] and the best fitted vector is 3x, what are all coefficient solutions? Is that set a vector space?
cards.answer: All (β₁,β₂) satisfying β₁+β₂=3: for example (3,0)+t(1,−1). The line does not contain zero, so it is affine but not a vector subspace. If the best fit were zero, the line β₁+β₂=0 would be the null space itself.
cards.takeaway: A nonzero fitted value shifts the solution set.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.27, printed p. 93

cards.title: Bounded multipliers do not bound every later entry by one.
cards.body: Partial pivoting gives multipliers of magnitude at most one. Does that prevent element growth in U?
cards.answer: No. Updates subtract a multiple of one row from another; magnitudes can grow when signs differ. For rows [1,−1] and [1,1], eliminating the first column produces a second entry 2 despite a multiplier of 1. Growth control is more subtle than the multiplier bound.
cards.takeaway: Subtraction can increase magnitude.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.27, printed p. 93 · companion practice

cards.title: The tangent formula has recognizable quartiles.
cards.body: For a Cauchy random variable with center m and scale γ, what samples correspond to U=0.25,0.5,0.75 under inverse-CDF sampling?
cards.answer: The formula m+γtan(π(U−1/2)) gives m−γ, m, and m+γ. These are the lower quartile, median, and upper quartile. Center is a median; the Cauchy mean is not defined.
cards.takeaway: A center parameter need not be an expectation.

cards.title: “Normal” does not mean Gaussian here.
cards.body:
Why are XᵀXβ̂ = Xᵀy called the normal equations?

Do you need normally distributed errors to derive them?
cards.answer:
Rearranging gives Xᵀ(y − Xβ̂) = 0: the residual is normal, or perpendicular, to every column of X. You can derive this by differentiating the squared-error objective or by projection geometry.

No distributional assumption is required to minimize ordinary squared error. Gaussian assumptions are used for particular likelihood and inference results.
cards.takeaway: The residual is perpendicular to the model space.

cards.title: The determinant has a sign to remember.
cards.body: Given PA = LU, where L has unit diagonal, how do you recover det(A) from U and the row swaps?
cards.answer:
Taking determinants gives det(P) det(A) = det(U), since det(L) = 1. Because det(P) is ±1, det(A) = det(P) ∏ᵢ uᵢᵢ. An odd number of row swaps changes the sign; an even number does not.

Agreement between two numerical determinant calculations is useful evidence, but it is not by itself a proof of accuracy.
cards.takeaway: Track the permutation, not just the diagonal.

cards.title: Inverse transforms have dangerous endpoints.
cards.body: Why should an inverse-Cauchy implementation avoid evaluating U exactly at 0 or 1?
cards.answer: The tangent argument becomes −π/2 or π/2, where the mathematical quantile is infinite. Numerical evaluation near these endpoints can yield enormous finite values. Use a generator and endpoint handling consistent with an open interval, and preserve the intended tail behavior rather than arbitrary clipping.
cards.takeaway: Endpoint conventions affect extreme draws.

cards.title: Expand the loss before taking its gradient.
cards.body: Expand S(β)=‖y−Xβ‖² and compute its gradient and Hessian.
cards.answer: S=yᵀy−2βᵀXᵀy+βᵀXᵀXβ. The gradient is −2Xᵀy+2XᵀXβ, and the Hessian is 2XᵀX. The Hessian is positive semidefinite, so a stationary point minimizes S; it is positive definite when X has full column rank.
cards.takeaway: Rank determines uniqueness, not existence of the projection.

cards.title: Why is a flat flag easier to compress?
cards.body:
Your homework compares a flat flag image with a photograph of a waving flag.

Why might the flat image need fewer rank-one pieces for a good approximation?
cards.answer:
Repeated stripes and repeated shapes make many rows or columns strongly related. A photograph adds folds, shading, perspective, and background detail, creating variation that needs more rank-one terms.

This is about good approximate rank, not necessarily small exact rank: pixel noise and image compression artifacts can make an image full rank.
cards.takeaway: Repeated structure is compressible.

cards.title: 50% acceptance is not 50% understanding.
cards.body:
Two random-walk samplers both accept half their proposals. One targets a round Gaussian; the other targets a Gaussian with correlation 0.99.

Must their sample quality be similar?
cards.answer:
No. The highly correlated target is a narrow, tilted ridge. Independent coordinate proposals may need tiny steps to avoid leaving it, moving slowly along the ridge even at 50% acceptance.

Inspect traces, autocorrelation, and exploration of the target. Acceptance rate alone does not measure effective independent information.
cards.takeaway: Mixing depends on geometry, too.

cards.title: An intercept forces the OLS residuals to sum to zero.
cards.body: If the design includes the ones vector, derive why Σeᵢ=0 at an ordinary least-squares solution.
cards.answer: The normal equations give Xᵀe=0. Taking the component corresponding to the intercept yields 1ᵀe=0. Without an intercept, this identity is not generally guaranteed. With weighted least squares, the relevant orthogonality is weighted.
cards.takeaway: Use the actual columns in the normal equations.

cards.title: Turn matrix error into per-pixel error.
cards.body: For an m×n image residual R, express RMS pixel error using the Frobenius norm.
cards.answer: RMS = √[ΣᵢⱼRᵢⱼ²/(mn)] = ‖R‖F/√(mn). If one image is stored on [0,255] and another on [0,1], their raw RMS errors are not directly comparable without accounting for the scale.
cards.takeaway: Normalize both dimensions and pixel units.

cards.title: Correlation makes one Gaussian direction narrow.
cards.body: For Σ=[[1,ρ],[ρ,1]], identify the eigen-directions and eigenvalues. What happens at ρ=0.99?
cards.answer: Directions (1,1) and (1,−1) have eigenvalues 1+ρ and 1−ρ. At 0.99 these are 1.99 and 0.01. Standard-deviation axis ratio is √199≈14.1. Independent equal-scale proposals do not naturally match this tilted geometry.
cards.takeaway: Target covariance determines useful proposal directions.

cards.title: The fit and residual are perpendicular.
cards.body: Given Xᵀe=0 and ŷ=Xβ̂, show ŷᵀe=0.
cards.answer: ŷᵀe=β̂ᵀXᵀe=0. Thus ‖y‖²=‖ŷ+e‖²=‖ŷ‖²+‖e‖². This is an uncentered identity; the usual decomposition around the sample mean additionally uses the intercept-space relationship.
cards.takeaway: Do not confuse centered and uncentered sums of squares.

cards.title: “Another rank-one update must reduce RMS error.”
cards.body: You use iterative Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting to approximate an image. Is the Frobenius error guaranteed to decrease after every update, as with truncated SVD?
cards.answer:
No. Complete pivoting greedily selects a largest-magnitude residual entry; it does not solve the best rank-k approximation problem in Frobenius norm. RMS error can rise on an intermediate update.

Truncated SVD does minimize Frobenius error for each rank, and its error is nonincreasing as more singular components are retained.
cards.takeaway: A greedy pivot is not an SVD guarantee.

cards.title: Nearly every move accepted can still be slow.
cards.body: Compare a random-walk proposal with a very tiny scale to one with a very large scale.
cards.answer: Tiny steps often accept but explore slowly because nearby states carry similar information. Huge steps often land in low-probability regions and reject, producing long holds. Tune for effective exploration of relevant quantities, not acceptance rate in isolation.
cards.takeaway: Movement distance and acceptance must be considered together.

cards.title: A projection done twice is still one projection.
cards.body: What two matrix identities characterize an orthogonal projection P in Euclidean space? Why is I − P also one?
cards.answer:
Symmetry: Pᵀ = P. Idempotence: P² = P. For the complement, (I − P)ᵀ = I − P and (I − P)² = I − 2P + P² = I − P.

P extracts the component in a subspace; I − P extracts the perpendicular component.
cards.takeaway: Symmetric + idempotent.

cards.title: One outer product clears a pivot row and column.
cards.body: A residual matrix R has a nonzero pivot Rᵢⱼ. Define U=R[:,j]R[i,:]/Rᵢⱼ. What happens to row i and column j of R−U in exact arithmetic?
cards.answer: U[i,:]=RᵢⱼR[i,:]/Rᵢⱼ=R[i,:], and U[:,j]=R[:,j]Rᵢⱼ/Rᵢⱼ=R[:,j]. Thus both vanish in the residual. U has rank at most one. Repeating this constructs a sum of rank-one approximations.
cards.takeaway: Elimination is a sequence of rank-one corrections.
cards.source: PS2 · Q2 · method comparison · companion practice

sources.locator: Lecture 03 · adaptive proposal discussion, companion caution

cards.title: Changing the kernel forever needs more theory.
cards.body: Why is tuning a proposal during a warm-up stage and then freezing it simpler to justify than unrestricted adaptation throughout sampling?
cards.answer: A fixed proposal after warm-up defines a fixed Markov kernel with the intended invariant target under the usual MH conditions. Continual history-dependent adaptation changes that setup and needs additional conditions for validity. Hitting a preferred acceptance rate alone is not a convergence proof.
cards.takeaway: Separate tuning from the samples used for inference.
cards.source: Lecture 03 · adaptive proposal discussion, companion caution · companion practice

cards.title: Projecting twice is not enough to mean perpendicular.
cards.body: P=[[1,1],[0,0]] satisfies P²=P. Is it an orthogonal projection?
cards.answer: No, since Pᵀ≠P. It maps onto the first coordinate axis along an oblique direction. For y=(0,1)ᵀ the fit is (1,0)ᵀ and residual (−1,1)ᵀ; their dot product is −1, not zero.
cards.takeaway: Idempotence gives a projection; symmetry makes it orthogonal.

cards.title: Stop before dividing by an all-zero residual.
cards.body: An iterative low-rank routine chooses the largest-magnitude residual entry and divides a row by that pivot. What should it do when that entry is zero?
cards.answer: If the largest magnitude is zero, the entire residual is zero: the approximation is already exact in the represented arithmetic. Stop rather than divide by zero. A numerical tolerance can support approximate stopping, but should be defined relative to the scale and intended error.
cards.takeaway: The pivot also supplies a stopping signal.
cards.source: PS2 · Q2 · method comparison · companion practice

cards.title: Stationary does not mean reversible.
cards.body: A three-state chain deterministically cycles A → B → C → A. The uniform distribution is stationary. Does it satisfy detailed balance?
cards.answer:
No. Uniform probability is preserved by the cycle, but probability flows from A to B and none flows directly from B to A. Detailed balance requires πᵢPᵢⱼ = πⱼPⱼᵢ for each pair.

It is sufficient for stationarity, not necessary. This example is also periodic, so a point-mass initial distribution does not converge to the uniform distribution.
cards.takeaway: Balanced totals can hide circulating flow.

cards.title: A projection’s eigenvalues can only be zero or one.
cards.body: If Pv=λv with v≠0 and P²=P, what equation must λ satisfy?
cards.answer: P²v=λ²v, but also P²v=Pv=λv. Hence λ²=λ, so λ is 0 or 1. For an orthogonal projector, the trace equals its rank because it counts eigenvalues equal to one.
cards.takeaway: Projection either retains or removes each eigen-direction.

cards.title: Curved shape. Linear unknowns.
cards.body:
For points (xᵢ, yᵢ), fit b x² + c xy + d y² ≈ 1.

What is one row of the design matrix? Why is this a linear least-squares problem?
cards.answer:
Row i is [xᵢ², xᵢyᵢ, yᵢ²], the parameter vector is [b, c, d]ᵀ, and the response is a vector of ones. The features can be nonlinear in the coordinates while the model remains linear in its unknown coefficients.

This minimizes algebraic residuals, not geometric distances to the curve.
cards.takeaway: Linear in parameters, not necessarily in inputs.

cards.title: Solve stationarity with flow and normalization.
cards.body: P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]]. Find the stationary distribution.
cards.answer: Let π=(a,b). Stationarity implies 0.2a=0.3b and a+b=1. Thus a=0.6,b=0.4. Multiplying πP verifies (0.6,0.4). Every irreducible two-state chain is reversible, but that does not extend to arbitrary larger chains.
cards.takeaway: Normalize the stationary flow relation.
cards.source: HW2 · Q2(b) · companion example · companion practice

cards.title: Degrees of freedom can be counted on the diagonal.
cards.body: An ordinary least-squares hat matrix H projects onto a rank-r model space. What are tr(H) and tr(I−H)?
cards.answer: They are r and n−r. The projector eigenvalues are 1 on the model space and 0 on its orthogonal complement. This counts fitted and residual dimensions without requiring the design to have independent columns.
cards.takeaway: Use model rank for fitted degrees of freedom.

cards.title: Coordinates become features.
cards.body: For a measured point (x,y)=(2,−3), what row belongs in the centered-ellipse design matrix for parameters (b,c,d)?
cards.answer: [x²,xy,y²]=[4,−6,9], with right-hand-side value 1. The model predicts 4b−6c+9d for that row. The cross-product feature keeps its sign; it is not |xy|.
cards.takeaway: Build each feature from the observed coordinates.

cards.title: Sum the pairwise balance equations.
cards.body: For a row-stochastic P, assume πᵢPᵢⱼ=πⱼPⱼᵢ for every i,j. Show that π is stationary.
cards.answer: Sum over i: ΣᵢπᵢPᵢⱼ=πⱼΣᵢPⱼᵢ=πⱼ because row j sums to one. Therefore πP=π. Stationarity only requires these total equalities; it does not force each pairwise equality separately.
cards.takeaway: Pairwise balance is stronger than total balance.
cards.source: HW2 · Q2(b) · companion example · companion practice

cards.title: Split the data into three perpendicular pieces.
cards.body: For nested model spaces V₀ ⊆ V₁ with orthogonal projectors P₀ and P₁, what do P₀y, (P₁ − P₀)y, and (I − P₁)y represent?
cards.answer:
They are the fit in the smaller model, the extra component captured by the larger model, and the residual outside the larger model. Nesting implies P₁P₀ = P₀P₁ = P₀, making the three projectors mutually orthogonal.

Their sum is I, so the three vectors add to y and their squared lengths add to ‖y‖².
cards.takeaway: Small fit + extra fit + residual.

cards.title: Small equation residual is not small Euclidean distance.
cards.body: A fit minimizes Σ(bxᵢ²+cxᵢyᵢ+dyᵢ²−1)². Is this the same as minimizing squared shortest distances from the points to the ellipse?
cards.answer: No. It penalizes the equation’s algebraic residual. Geometric distance requires finding nearest points on the curve, a nonlinear problem. The algebraic formulation is computationally convenient but gives a different loss and can weight locations differently.
cards.takeaway: Name the loss you actually minimized.

cards.title: An invariant distribution need not attract every start.
cards.body: A chain alternates deterministically between two states. Its uniform distribution is stationary. Do marginals from a fixed starting state converge to it?
cards.answer: No. The chain has period two and alternates between point masses. Starting in the uniform distribution preserves it, but starting at one state causes persistent oscillation. For finite chains, irreducibility and aperiodicity provide the usual convergence guarantee.
cards.takeaway: Invariant and limiting distributions are distinct concepts.
cards.source: HW2 · Q2(b) · companion example · companion practice

cards.title: Projecting a smaller-space vector onto the larger space does nothing.
cards.body: If V₀⊆V₁, why are P₁P₀=P₀ and P₀P₁=P₀ for orthogonal projectors?
cards.answer: P₀v already lies in V₀ and therefore V₁, so P₁P₀v=P₀v for every v. Taking transposes and using symmetry gives P₀P₁=P₀ as well. The second identity follows from orthogonality; do not assume projectors always commute.
cards.takeaway: Nesting supplies the useful product identities.

cards.title: A fitted quadratic is not automatically an ellipse.
cards.body: Your least-squares solver returns b, c, d. Before plotting b x² + c xy + d y² = 1 as an ellipse, what should you check?
cards.answer:
Form Q = [[b, c/2], [c/2, d]]. For a real nondegenerate ellipse with right-hand side 1, Q must be positive definite. Equivalently, b > 0 and bd − c²/4 > 0.

An unconstrained algebraic fit does not enforce this. Other coefficients can describe a hyperbola, a degenerate curve, or no real points.
cards.takeaway: Validate the geometry after fitting.

cards.title: What you hide can bring back memory.
cards.body:
Alice sends the ball to Carol with probability 2/3; Bob sends it to Carol with probability 1/2. You record only “Carol” or “not Carol.”

Why is the coarsened process not guaranteed to be Markov?
cards.answer:
The hidden identity inside “not Carol” affects the next-step probability of Carol. History can change whether Alice or Bob is likely to hold the ball, so the current coarse state may not contain enough information.

For strong lumpability, every state within a block must have the same total transition probability into each other block. Here 2/3 ≠ 1/2.
cards.takeaway: A state must retain the relevant information.

cards.title: Subtracting arbitrary projectors need not give a projector.
cards.body: Let P₀=diag(1,0) and P₁=diag(0,1). Is P₁−P₀ an orthogonal projector?
cards.answer: No. P₁−P₀=diag(−1,1), whose square is I rather than itself. The familiar extra-sum-of-squares projector requires nested model spaces, which these coordinate axes are not.
cards.takeaway: Check nesting before using a difference of projectors.

cards.title: The off-diagonal entries each contribute half.
cards.body: Why is the quadratic-form matrix for bx²+cxy+dy² equal to [[b,c/2],[c/2,d]] rather than [[b,c],[c,d]]?
cards.answer: Expanding [x,y]Q[x,y]ᵀ gives Q₁₁x²+(Q₁₂+Q₂₁)xy+Q₂₂y². With symmetry, the two equal off-diagonal contributions must sum to c, so each is c/2.
cards.takeaway: Expand the quadratic form to verify coefficients.

cards.title: Sometimes a coarse state retains enough information.
cards.body: States A and B are combined. If both send total probability 0.4 to block C and 0.6 to block {A,B}, does their different internal A/B behavior prevent strong lumpability?
cards.answer: Not for this two-block partition. Their total outgoing probability to each block agrees, so the next coarse state does not depend on which hidden member currently holds. Internal transitions may differ while the block-level process remains Markov.
cards.takeaway: Compare probabilities to blocks, not individual destinations.

cards.title: Same model. A different intercept.
cards.body: With treatment coding, what does the intercept represent? With sum coding, what does it represent? Assume other numeric predictors are zero.
cards.answer:
Treatment coding: the fitted mean of the reference group. Sum coding: the equally weighted average of the fitted group means, because the group deviations sum to zero.

This is not generally the sample-size-weighted overall mean. With an intercept and equivalent full-rank coding, the group predictions remain unchanged.
cards.takeaway: Coding changes the question each coefficient answers.

cards.title: Eigenvalues reveal the ellipse’s axis lengths.
cards.body: If a positive-definite quadratic form Q has eigenvalues 4 and 1/9, what are the semiaxis lengths of zᵀQz=1?
cards.answer: In Q’s orthonormal eigenbasis, the equation is 4u²+(1/9)v²=1. The semiaxes are 1/√4=1/2 and 1/√(1/9)=3. Large quadratic-form eigenvalues correspond to short axes, not long ones.
cards.takeaway: Quadratic-form axes use inverse square roots.

cards.title: Straighten the uncertainty before measuring it.
cards.body: A Gaussian vector has positive-definite covariance Σ. Why transform y to z = Σ⁻¹ᐟ²(y − μ)?
cards.answer:
The transformed vector has mean zero and covariance I. For a Gaussian it is standard multivariate normal, and ‖z‖² = (y − μ)ᵀΣ⁻¹(y − μ) has a chi-squared distribution with dimension-many degrees of freedom.

This same geometry explains why covariance-aware coordinates can help a sampler explore a narrow correlated Gaussian. A parameter transformation in general also requires the appropriate density Jacobian.
cards.takeaway: Whitening measures distance in uncertainty units.

cards.title: Decode three group means from treatment coding.
cards.body: At a fixed numeric predictor value, suppose the reference fitted mean is 10 and treatment coefficients for B and C are 2 and −3. What are the fitted group means?
cards.answer: A:10, B:12, C:7. The two coefficients are differences from the reference, not absolute group means. If an additional baseline term contributes 4 at this predictor value, add it to all three means.
cards.takeaway: Separate the shared part from the group contrast.

cards.title: Uniform radius crowds the center.
cards.body: To sample uniformly by area inside a disk, why use r = √U instead of r = U, with a uniform angle?
cards.answer:
The fraction of disk area inside radius r is πr²/π = r². Thus the desired radius CDF is F(r) = r² on [0,1], and inverse-transform sampling gives r = √U.

A uniform radius assigns too much probability to inner rings, whose areas are smaller. This connects AM 205’s disk experiment to AM 207’s transformations and Jacobians.
cards.takeaway: Uniform area is not uniform radius.

cards.title: Two random draws. One reaction.
cards.body:
A system has propensities a₁ = 2 and a₂ = 3 per second.

What is the mean waiting time until the next event, and the probability that event is reaction 2?
cards.answer:
Total propensity is a₀ = 5 per second. The waiting time is exponential with mean 1/5 = 0.2 seconds. Reaction 2 is selected with probability a₂/a₀ = 3/5.

After applying the selected reaction, recompute propensities. If a₀ = 0, no further reactions are possible at the current state.
cards.takeaway: When: total rate. Which: relative rates.

cards.title: The omitted deviation is minus the others.
cards.body: A three-level sum-coded model has intercept 10 and two displayed effects 2 and −1. What is the third effect and the three group means at zero numeric predictors?
cards.answer: The third effect is −(2−1)=−1. The means are 12,9,9, whose equally weighted average is 10. This average is over levels, not over their observed sample sizes.
cards.takeaway: Sum-to-zero coding fixes the missing deviation.

cards.title: Before solving it, ask whether it is well posed.
cards.body: What three properties define a well-posed computational problem?
cards.answer: A solution exists; it is unique; and it depends continuously on the data. Ill-conditioning concerns sensitivity even when these conditions hold. An ill-posed problem may need reformulation, constraints, or regularization before numerical computation is meaningful.
cards.takeaway: Existence, uniqueness, continuous dependence.

cards.title: Carry out one direct-SSA event.
cards.body: Current propensities are (1,3,6), U₁=e⁻², and U₂=0.35. What waiting time and reaction are selected?
cards.answer: Total rate is 10, so τ=−log(e⁻²)/10=0.2. The cumulative reaction probabilities are 0.1,0.4,1. Since 0.35 lies in the second interval, select reaction 2. Update the state, then recompute affected propensities.
cards.takeaway: One draw sets the time; the other chooses the channel.

cards.title: A contrast column’s scale changes its coefficient.
cards.body: For the R-style three-group Helmert coding in HW2, why is the first coefficient half the B−A mean difference?
cards.answer: The first contrast takes values −1 for A, +1 for B, and 0 for C. Subtracting the A mean from the B mean gives 2γ₁. The second column takes −1,−1,+2, so C minus the average of A and B equals 3γ₂. Always inspect the coding matrix.
cards.takeaway: Contrast coefficients depend on column normalization.

cards.title: More precision does not fix a wrong model.
cards.body: Distinguish modeling error, discretization error, rounding error, and uncertainty already in the input data.
cards.answer:
Modeling error comes from how the mathematical model approximates reality. Discretization replaces an infinite or continuous computation with a finite approximation. Rounding uses a finite set of machine numbers. Input uncertainty exists before the algorithm starts.

More arithmetic precision directly addresses rounding, not all four sources.
cards.takeaway: Identify the source before choosing the remedy.

cards.title: Do not apply an event after the requested end time.
cards.body: Your current time is 9.8, the simulation horizon is 10, and the sampled waiting time is 0.5. What should you record at time 10?
cards.answer: The current state remains unchanged through time 10 because the next event would occur at 10.3. Do not apply that event and label its state as occurring within the horizon. Correct handling matters for endpoint summaries and time-weighted statistics.
cards.takeaway: An event’s state update belongs at its actual event time.

cards.title: Equivalent contrasts may stop being equivalent without the intercept.
cards.body: Treatment, sum, and Helmert coding span the same factor model when correctly augmented with an intercept. Can you automatically drop the intercept from each and keep that equivalence?
cards.answer: No. Sum and Helmert columns span zero-sum contrasts across levels, while treatment columns have a different span before adding the intercept. The augmented spaces coincide; the unaugmented spaces need not. Compare the actual column spaces after the change.
cards.takeaway: Equivalence depends on the full design matrix.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.50, printed p. 41

cards.title: A smaller step can make the computation worse.
cards.body: For a forward difference [f(x+h)−f(x)]/h, why can decreasing h eventually increase the error?
cards.answer: Truncation error typically decreases like O(h), but rounding and function-evaluation errors in the numerator can be amplified by division by h, giving a term of order u/h under a simple scale model. Extremely small h may also make x+h round to x. Balance both errors rather than shrinking h indefinitely.
cards.takeaway: Convergence in exact arithmetic is only part of the story.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.50, printed p. 41 · companion practice

cards.title: Zero total propensity means no next event.
cards.body: All reaction propensities at the current state are zero. Should the SSA compute −log(U)/0 or choose a random reaction anyway?
cards.answer: No. With no allowed reactions, the state is absorbing under the current time-homogeneous reaction model. Advance the record to the horizon without a reaction or stop. If rates have external time dependence, a separate algorithm must account for future changes.
cards.takeaway: No available channel means no jump.

cards.title: SSE divided by n—or by n minus p?
cards.body: For a full-column-rank Gaussian linear model with n observations and p fitted coefficients, compare the maximum-likelihood and unbiased estimates of σ².
cards.answer:
The MLE is SSE/n (assuming positive residual sum of squares). The unbiased estimate is SSE/(n − p), because E[SSE] = (n − p)σ² under the model.

More generally, use n − rank(X) residual degrees of freedom. The MLE optimizes likelihood; unbiasedness is a different criterion.
cards.takeaway: Likelihood and unbiasedness are different goals.

cards.title: An exact subtraction can expose inaccurate inputs.
cards.body: Suppose two large approximate quantities share many leading digits. Why can their difference have large relative error even if the final machine subtraction is exact?
cards.answer: The true difference can be much smaller than either operand. Preexisting operand errors then become large relative to that difference. Cancellation removes matching leading digits; it does not have to introduce fresh rounding in the subtraction itself.
cards.takeaway: Track the errors already present in the operands.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Two identical reactants must be counted as pairs.
cards.body: For reaction 2A→B with per-unordered-pair rate c and n A molecules, what is the propensity?
cards.answer: c·C(n,2)=c n(n−1)/2. At n=1 it is zero. Using cn² would allow self-pairing and overcount ordered pairs. Rate-constant conventions can absorb factors, so state the convention before comparing formulas.
cards.takeaway: Count distinct reacting combinations.

cards.title: The likelihood estimate and unbiased estimate differ.
cards.body: For n=20, rank(X)=4, and SSE=80, calculate the Gaussian MLE and unbiased estimate of σ².
cards.answer: MLE:80/20=4. Unbiased estimate:80/(20−4)=5. Their difference reflects the four fitted directions consuming residual degrees of freedom. Under the model E[SSE]=16σ², so dividing by 20 biases downward.
cards.takeaway: The denominator encodes the criterion.
cards.source: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion practice

cards.title: Rewrite before subtracting nearly equal numbers.
cards.body: For small positive x, how can you evaluate √(1+x)−1 without directly subtracting two nearly equal numbers?
cards.answer: Multiply numerator and denominator by √(1+x)+1 to obtain x/[√(1+x)+1]. The denominator is near 2, so this avoids subtracting nearly equal terms. Algebraically equivalent expressions can behave very differently in floating-point arithmetic.
cards.takeaway: Choose a form that avoids unnecessary cancellation.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: The average of a product is not the product of averages.
cards.body: A reaction rate contains RF, the product of rabbit and fox counts. Why can the exact equation for E[F] depend on more than E[R] and E[F]?
cards.answer:
Because E[RF] = E[R]E[F] + Cov(R,F). The exact mean equation can therefore involve second moments. Their equations can involve still higher moments.

Replacing E[RF] by E[R]E[F] is a mean-field closure assumption, not a general identity. In the urn model, linear drift permits a closed mean equation without this replacement.
cards.takeaway: Nonlinearity couples the moments.

cards.title: Differentiate with respect to variance, not standard deviation.
cards.body: Let s=σ² and R=SSE>0. For ℓ(s)=−(n/2)log s−R/(2s)+constant, verify the curvature at ŝ=R/n.
cards.answer: ℓ′(s)=−n/(2s)+R/(2s²). Then ℓ″(s)=n/(2s²)−R/s³. Substituting ŝ=R/n gives −n³/(2R²)<0. If R=0, there is no positive interior maximizer of this form; the variance tends toward the boundary.
cards.takeaway: Name the parameter before differentiating.
cards.source: HW2 · Q7; least-squares theory · companion practice

cards.title: An intermediate can overflow even when the answer fits.
cards.body: Why can directly computing √(a²+b²) fail for a=b=10³⁰⁰ in binary64, and how can you rewrite it?
cards.answer: Squaring either input overflows, although the norm is about 1.414×10³⁰⁰ and is representable. Let m=max(|a|,|b|); for m>0 compute m√[(a/m)²+(b/m)²]. Return zero when m=0. Scaling keeps the squared terms at most one.
cards.takeaway: Check intermediates, not just the final range.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Quantify the mean-field error in a product.
cards.body: E[R]=10, E[F]=4, and Cov(R,F)=−6. Compare E[RF] with the mean-field replacement E[R]E[F].
cards.answer: E[RF]=10·4−6=34. The product-of-means approximation is 40, overestimating this moment by 6. Positive covariance would reverse the direction. The error is not determined by the marginal means alone.
cards.takeaway: The omitted covariance has both magnitude and sign.
cards.source: HW2 · Q3(c) and Q4(a–b) · companion practice

cards.title: “Best” comes with a comparison class.
cards.body: Gauss–Markov calls ordinary least squares BLUE. Does that mean it beats every possible estimator or requires Gaussian errors?
cards.answer:
Neither. With full-column-rank X, E[y] = Xβ, and Var(y) = σ²I, OLS has minimum variance among estimators that are linear in y and unbiased for the target. Normality is not required.

Biased or nonlinear estimators are outside this comparison class. “Best” does not promise the lowest test error for every prediction task.
cards.takeaway: Best linear unbiased—not universally best.

cards.title: Infinity and NaN mean different failures.
cards.body: Under usual IEEE floating-point semantics, distinguish nonzero finite division by zero from 0/0. How should a downstream comparison treat NaN?
cards.answer: Nonzero finite division by zero yields a signed infinity (depending on the language’s exception behavior); 0/0 is invalid and produces NaN. NaN does not compare equal to itself, so use a dedicated isnan check rather than x==NaN. Language-level operators may raise exceptions instead of returning these values.
cards.takeaway: Understand both IEEE semantics and language behavior.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review, printed pp. 40–41 · companion practice

cards.title: Four heads does not make the probability exactly 4/11.
cards.body:
Observe 4 heads in 11 independent tosses of a coin with unknown head probability θ. Start with a uniform prior on θ.

What is the posterior distribution?
cards.answer:
The likelihood is proportional to θ⁴(1 − θ)⁷. A uniform prior is Beta(1,1), so the posterior is Beta(5,8). Its mean is 5/13 and its mode is 4/11.

The posterior expresses uncertainty over θ; a point estimate alone does not. This is a derived companion calculation to the lecture coin example.
cards.takeaway: Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior.

cards.title: Which conclusions need normality?
cards.body: Separate these claims: OLS is unbiased; OLS is BLUE; coefficient t statistics have exact t distributions.
cards.answer: Unbiasedness follows from E[y]=Xβ and a full-rank fixed design. BLUE additionally needs the spherical covariance condition σ²I for ordinary OLS. Exact finite-sample t reference distributions use Gaussian errors as well. Without normality, asymptotic inference may still be possible under additional conditions.
cards.takeaway: Use only the assumptions each conclusion needs.

cards.title: One millimeter can be tiny—or enormous.
cards.body: An estimate is 0.002 and the exact value is 0.001. Find the absolute and relative errors. What changes when the exact value is zero?
cards.answer: Absolute error is |0.002 − 0.001| = 0.001. Relative error is 0.001 / 0.001 = 1, or 100%. Relative error divided by the exact value is undefined when that value is zero; use an absolute tolerance or a meaningful external scale instead.
cards.takeaway: Absolute error needs scale to be interpretable.

cards.title: Prior counts and observed counts combine.
cards.body: If θ∼Beta(a,b) and you observe h heads and t tails in independent Bernoulli trials, what is the posterior?
cards.answer: Beta(a+h,b+t), because the prior contributes θ^(a−1)(1−θ)^(b−1) and the likelihood contributes θ^h(1−θ)^t. The posterior mean is (a+h)/(a+b+h+t). This applies when the trials share the same θ and the stated conditional-independence model.
cards.takeaway: Multiply kernels and recognize the distribution.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: An inverse identity can survive singularity.
cards.body: For a matrix B, what identity defines a generalized inverse G in the sense used in your notes? Is G necessarily unique?
cards.answer:
BGB = B. Such a G need not be unique. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse adds further conditions and is unique.

Do not freely replace BG or GB with the identity: that is an ordinary-inverse property and generally fails for a singular matrix.
cards.takeaway: BGB = B does not imply BG = I.

cards.title: Correct answer. Slightly different question.
cards.body: Approximate √2 by 1.4. What is the absolute forward error? What input makes 1.4 an exact square root?
cards.answer:
Forward error is |1.4 − √2| ≈ 0.0142. Since 1.4² = 1.96, the result is exact for the nearby input 1.96, with absolute backward error |1.96 − 2| = 0.04.

Backward error asks how much the input would need to change to justify the computed result.
cards.takeaway: Forward: output error. Backward: input perturbation.

cards.title: Prediction averages over parameter uncertainty.
cards.body: After observing 4 heads and 7 tails with a uniform prior, what is the posterior probability of a head on the next exchangeable toss?
cards.answer: The posterior is Beta(5,8). Integrating θ against it gives P(next head|data)=E[θ|data]=5/13≈0.3846. This is a predictive probability, distinct from the posterior mode 4/11 or a claim that θ equals one number with certainty.
cards.takeaway: Posterior prediction integrates the unknown parameter.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: A generalized inverse can have a free entry.
cards.body: For B=diag(1,0), show that G=diag(1,t) is a generalized inverse for any real t. Which t gives its Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse?
cards.answer: BGB=diag(1,0)=B for every t. The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse is diag(1,0), so t=0. The extra Moore–Penrose conditions remove freedoms left by BGB=B.
cards.takeaway: The sandwich condition alone does not imply uniqueness.
cards.source: Linear algebra notes · pp. 4–5 · companion practice

cards.title: The residual is an input perturbation.
cards.body: Let r=b−Ax̂. If you keep A fixed, for what perturbed right-hand side is x̂ an exact solution?
cards.answer: Ax̂=b−r, so the perturbed right-hand side is b̃=b−r. The backward change is Δb=−r. For nonzero b, ‖r‖/‖b‖ is the relative right-hand-side perturbation. This concerns a square solve; a least-squares residual can be nonzero even at the exact minimizer.
cards.takeaway: A residual can describe a nearby problem.

cards.title: A likelihood is a function of the parameter, not automatically its density.
cards.body: Why is p(data|θ) not automatically the posterior density p(θ|data)?
cards.answer: The posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior, normalized over θ. A likelihood treats the observed data as fixed while varying θ; it need not integrate to one over θ. Reversing the conditional requires Bayes’ rule, not just renaming the arguments.
cards.takeaway: The conditioning direction matters.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: Check a proposed generalized inverse by sandwiching it.
cards.body: Let A be invertible and G a generalized inverse of B. Show that A⁻¹G is a valid generalized inverse of BA.
cards.answer:
Compute (BA)(A⁻¹G)(BA) = BGB A = BA. That is exactly the required sandwich identity.

This constructs a valid choice; it does not assert that every generalized inverse of BA must equal this one.
cards.takeaway: Verify the defining identity directly.

cards.title: “A stable solver fixes an ill-conditioned problem.”
cards.body: Why can a backward-stable algorithm still return an inaccurate solution?
cards.answer:
Backward stability makes the result exact for slightly perturbed data. An ill-conditioned problem can amplify that small perturbation into a large output change. Roughly, relative forward error is bounded by conditioning times relative backward error in an appropriate local analysis.

Conditioning describes the problem; stability describes the algorithm.
cards.takeaway: Small backward error can become large forward error.

cards.title: The binomial coefficient may cancel for estimation but not for evidence.
cards.body: For h heads in n flips, compare the likelihood of one specified sequence with the likelihood of the unordered count h.
cards.answer: A specified sequence has probability θ^h(1−θ)^(n−h). The count has C(n,h) times that probability. The coefficient does not depend on θ, so both produce the same normalized posterior shape under the same prior. Their data-event probabilities differ, so the factor can matter for evidence calculations.
cards.takeaway: Constants can be irrelevant for one task and essential for another.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 45–51 · companion calculation · companion practice

cards.title: The inverse factor changes sides with the product.
cards.body: If G is a generalized inverse of B and A is invertible, verify that GA⁻¹ is a generalized inverse of AB.
cards.answer: (AB)(GA⁻¹)(AB) = ABG(A⁻¹A)B = ABGB = A(BGB) = AB. Thus GA⁻¹ is a generalized inverse of AB when BGB = B and A is invertible.
cards.takeaway: Reassociation is allowed; reordering is not.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.64–65, printed p. 95

cards.title: How many digits might sensitivity consume?
cards.body: A backward-stable solve uses data accurate to roughly 12 decimal digits, and κ(A)≈10⁴. Roughly how many accurate digits might remain?
cards.answer: About 8 digits in a typical first-order worst-case estimate: relative error scales like 10⁴×10⁻¹²=10⁻⁸. This is a heuristic bound, not a promise; the direction of data error and solver constants matter.
cards.takeaway: Conditioning can amplify error by orders of magnitude.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.64–65, printed p. 95 · companion practice

cards.title: A density greater than one is allowed.
cards.body: X is uniform on [0, 0.2], so its density is 5 there. Does this violate the rule that probabilities are at most one?
cards.answer: No. Probability is the integral of density over a set. Here the total area is 5 × 0.2 = 1. A density has units of inverse x-units; its height is not itself an event probability. For a continuous distribution, a single point has probability zero.
cards.takeaway: Probability is area, not density height.

cards.title: The coefficients can vary while the projection stays fixed.
cards.body: Why does XGXᵀ give the same fitted-value projector for every generalized inverse G of XᵀX?
cards.answer:
On C(X), the operator XGXᵀ acts as the identity; on C(X)⊥, Xᵀv = 0, so it acts as zero. Every observation vector decomposes uniquely into those two subspaces.

Thus the action on every vector is fixed even if G and the coefficient estimate are not unique.
cards.takeaway: Unique fitted values do not require unique coefficients.

cards.title: Sensitivity has a derivative.
cards.body: For a differentiable scalar function y=f(x), with x and f(x) nonzero, derive its local relative condition number.
cards.answer: For a small input perturbation Δx, Δy≈f′(x)Δx. Divide output relative error by input relative error: |Δy/f(x)| / |Δx/x| ≈ |x f′(x)/f(x)|. The formula needs care near zeros of x or f, where this relative scaling is undefined or misleading.
cards.takeaway: Relative conditioning compares relative changes.

cards.title: Recover interval probability from a CDF.
cards.body: If a continuous random variable has F(1)=0.2 and F(3)=0.8, what is P(1<X≤3)? Is it the density at 3?
cards.answer: The probability is F(3)−F(1)=0.6. A density is the local derivative of an absolutely continuous CDF where the derivative exists. A CDF difference accumulates probability over an interval; a density value alone does not.
cards.takeaway: Use CDF differences for interval probabilities.

cards.title: Different coefficients, identical fitted vector.
cards.body: For X=[[1,0],[1,0]], y=(1,3)ᵀ, describe the fitted values and all least-squares coefficient vectors.
cards.answer: The first coefficient is the mean, β₁=2, while β₂ is arbitrary because its column is zero. All fits are (2,2)ᵀ, and the residual is (−1,1)ᵀ. Any valid least-squares solution gives the same projection.
cards.takeaway: Unused coefficient directions cannot change the fit.

cards.title: Square roots damp relative input errors.
cards.body: For f(x)=√x and x>0, compute |x f′(x)/f(x)|.
cards.answer: Since f′(x)=1/(2√x), the relative condition number is x/(2x)=1/2. A small relative input error produces about half as much relative output error locally. Absolute sensitivity, 1/(2√x), is a different measure and grows near zero.
cards.takeaway: Absolute and relative sensitivity can tell different stories.

cards.title: A candidate density needs total mass one.
cards.body: Let f(x)=cx on [0,2] and zero elsewhere. Find c and then P(X≤1).
cards.answer: Normalization gives ∫₀²cx dx=2c=1, so c=1/2. Then P(X≤1)=∫₀¹x/2 dx=1/4. A function being nonnegative is necessary but not enough to make it a density.
cards.takeaway: Check nonnegativity and normalization.

cards.title: Why the projected fit is closest.
cards.body: Let μ̂ be the orthogonal projection of y onto C(X). For any μ in C(X), explain why ‖y−μ‖² ≥ ‖y−μ̂‖².
cards.answer:
Write y−μ = (y−μ̂) + (μ̂−μ). The first term is perpendicular to C(X); the second lies in it. Therefore the cross term is zero and ‖y−μ‖² = ‖y−μ̂‖² + ‖μ̂−μ‖².

The last term is nonnegative. This proves the claim without differentiating.
cards.takeaway: Perpendicular pieces make squared lengths add.

cards.title: Same numbers. Different parentheses.
cards.body: In binary64, compare (10¹⁶ + (−10¹⁶)) + 1 with 10¹⁶ + ((−10¹⁶) + 1).
cards.answer:
The first evaluates to 1. In the second, the addition of 1 to −10¹⁶ rounds back to −10¹⁶ under round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, so the result is 0.

Floating-point addition is not associative. Parallel reductions or reordered sums can therefore give different answers.
cards.takeaway: Parentheses can change floating-point results.

cards.title: Average the function under the distribution.
cards.body: For a continuous X with density p, what is E[g(X)]? Do you first need the distribution of Y=g(X)?
cards.answer: E[g(X)]=∫g(x)p(x)dx when the expectation exists. You can compute it directly under X without deriving Y’s density. For discrete X, replace the integral by a weighted sum. This is the basis of many Monte Carlo estimators.
cards.takeaway: Transform the integrand before transforming the distribution.

cards.title: Every competing unbiased estimator adds variance.
cards.body: Write another linear unbiased estimator as By, where B = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ + A. Why must AX = 0, and what happens to its variance?
cards.answer:
Unbiasedness for every β requires BX = I, so AX = BX−I = 0. Under Var(y)=σ²I, the cross terms vanish and Var(By) = σ²(XᵀX)⁻¹ + σ²AAᵀ.

AAᵀ is positive semidefinite, so every linear contrast has at least the OLS variance.
cards.takeaway: The extra component has nonnegative variance.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.45–49, printed p. 41

cards.title: Small terms can disappear into a large partial sum.
cards.body: When summing positive numbers of very different magnitudes, why can adding smaller terms first help?
cards.answer: A small addend may be below half the spacing of a large partial sum and round away. Combining small terms first can let them accumulate into a representable contribution. Pairwise or compensated summation can also help. No ordering is a universal optimality guarantee for arbitrary signed data.
cards.takeaway: Preserve small contributions before the scale grows.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 1 review Q1.45–49, printed p. 41 · companion practice

cards.title: Conditioning changes the denominator.
cards.body: A fair six-sided die is known to show an even result. What is the probability that it shows a value greater than 3?
cards.answer: The conditional possibilities are {2,4,6}; two exceed 3. The probability is 2/3, or P({4,6})/P({2,4,6})=(2/6)/(3/6). Conditioning restricts and renormalizes the sample space.
cards.takeaway: The denominator is the probability of the information.
cards.source: Lecture 01 · conditional probability example · companion practice

cards.title: Show the variance gap for one estimable contrast.
cards.body: A competing linear unbiased estimate of ℓᵀβ has weights a=X(XᵀX)⁻¹ℓ+z with Xᵀz=0. What is its excess variance over the OLS contrast?
cards.answer: Under Var(y)=σ²I, Var(aᵀy)=σ²aᵀa. The cross term is zero because ℓᵀ(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀz=0. The excess is σ²zᵀz≥0, with equality when z=0.
cards.takeaway: The perpendicular extra component contributes nonnegative variance.

cards.title: Many printed digits are not many correct digits.
cards.body: What is the difference between arithmetic precision and accuracy of a computed result?
cards.answer:
Precision describes the representational capacity of the arithmetic. Accuracy describes closeness to the desired answer. High precision can reduce rounding error, but cannot recover missing input information or make a poor model correct.

Printing 16 digits does not establish that all 16 are meaningful.
