cards.takeaway: Representation capacity is not an accuracy certificate.

cards.title: Disjoint events usually are not independent.
cards.body: If A and B are disjoint and each has positive probability, can they be independent?
cards.answer: No. Disjointness gives P(A∩B)=0, whereas independence would require P(A)P(B)>0. Learning that A happened rules out B, which is strong dependence. An event of probability zero is an exceptional case.
cards.takeaway: Mutual exclusion is different from independence.
cards.source: Lecture 01 · probability rules, companion example · companion practice

cards.title: Unequal uncertainty calls for a different distance.
cards.body: If Var(y)=σ²V with known positive-definite V, what replaces ordinary squared residual length?
cards.answer:
Minimize (y−Xβ)ᵀV⁻¹(y−Xβ). This is ordinary least squares after whitening y and X by V⁻¹ᐟ². For full-column-rank X, β̂ = (XᵀV⁻¹X)⁻¹XᵀV⁻¹y.

The residual is orthogonal to C(X) under the V⁻¹-weighted inner product, not necessarily under the ordinary Euclidean one.
cards.takeaway: Whiten, then project.

cards.title: A tiny determinant can be harmless.
cards.body: For A = 10⁻¹⁰ I₂, compare det(A) with its 2-norm condition number. Is A ill-conditioned?
cards.answer:
det(A) = 10⁻²⁰, but κ₂(A) = σmax/σmin = 1. Both singular values are 10⁻¹⁰. Uniform scaling makes the determinant tiny without making the solve sensitive to relative perturbations.

Determinant magnitude alone is a poor near-singularity diagnostic.
cards.takeaway: Conditioning is about relative stretching.

cards.title: Stretching values thins the density.
cards.body: If Y = 2X and X has density fX, what is fY(y)? Why is the factor 1/2 needed?
cards.answer:
fY(y) = fX(y/2)/2. The mapping doubles interval lengths, so density must halve to preserve probability mass. The inverse-map derivative has magnitude |dx/dy| = 1/2.

For a differentiable one-to-one transformation, multiply by the absolute determinant of the inverse Jacobian.
cards.takeaway: Preserve mass when coordinates change.

cards.title: Verify that the transformed errors are spherical.
cards.body: If Var(y)=σ²V and A=V⁻¹ᐟ² is the symmetric inverse square root, calculate Var(Ay).
cards.answer: Var(Ay)=A(σ²V)Aᵀ=σ²V⁻¹ᐟ²VV⁻¹ᐟ²=σ²I. Transform X with the same A so the mean becomes AXβ. Whitening only the response while leaving X unchanged defines a different model.
cards.takeaway: Transform both response and design.

cards.title: Column sums and row sums measure different amplification.
cards.body: For A=[[1,−2],[3,4]], compute ‖A‖₁ and ‖A‖∞.
cards.answer: The induced 1-norm is the maximum absolute column sum: max(1+3,2+4)=6. The infinity-norm is the maximum absolute row sum: max(1+2,3+4)=7. Taking the sum of every entry’s magnitude is neither of these induced norms.
cards.takeaway: One-norm: columns. Infinity-norm: rows.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · matrix norms · companion practice

cards.title: The absolute value keeps the density nonnegative.
cards.body: If Y=−3X, express fY(y) in terms of fX.
cards.answer: The inverse is x=−y/3 with derivative −1/3. Thus fY(y)=fX(−y/3)/3. The sign reverses orientation, while the absolute derivative rescales probability density. Forgetting the absolute value would produce a negative density.
cards.takeaway: Orientation changes do not make negative probability.

cards.title: More precise observations get more weight.
cards.body: Two independent measurements have variances σ² and 4σ². What relative weights should weighted least squares use?
cards.answer:
Weights are proportional to inverse variance: 1 and 1/4. The noisier measurement receives less weight.

For an average of m independent equal-variance observations, variance is σ²/m, so the corresponding precision weight is m.
cards.takeaway: Weight by precision, not by variance.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.57, printed p. 94

cards.title: Compare largest and smallest scaling factors.
cards.body: For D=diag(4,−6,2), what is its condition number in the induced 1-, 2-, and infinity-norms?
cards.answer: All three give 6/(2)=3. The norm is the largest diagonal magnitude, 6; the inverse norm is the largest reciprocal magnitude, 1/2. The negative sign changes orientation along a coordinate, not the magnitude ratio.
cards.takeaway: For a diagonal matrix, use absolute diagonal values.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.57, printed p. 94 · companion practice

cards.title: A determinant measures local area scaling.
cards.body: If Y=AX for an invertible 2×2 matrix A, what is the transformed density?
cards.answer: fY(y)=fX(A⁻¹y)|det(A⁻¹)|=fX(A⁻¹y)/|det(A)|. A small area element grows by |det(A)|, so density changes by its reciprocal. If A is singular, this ordinary two-dimensional density formula does not apply.
cards.takeaway: Match the Jacobian to the dimension of the density.

cards.title: Compute the best constant when precision differs.
cards.body: For independent observations y₁=2 and y₂=8 with known variances proportional to 1 and 4, what weighted least-squares constant do you fit?
cards.answer: Use weights 1 and 1/4. The fitted constant is (1·2+(1/4)·8)/(1+1/4)=4/1.25=3.2. The noisier value 8 has less influence. The unweighted mean 5 answers a different optimization problem.
cards.takeaway: Precision weights pull toward the more reliable measurement.

cards.title: A tiny residual is not the whole answer.
cards.body: You compute x̂ with small residual r = b − Ax̂. What additional issue matters before concluding that x̂ is close to the true x?
cards.answer:
Check scaling and conditioning. The residual changes if you scale both A and b, even though the true solution does not. And x̂ − x = −A⁻¹r, so an ill-conditioned system can amplify a small residual.

Use a scaled residual together with a condition estimate.
cards.takeaway: Small residual + good conditioning supports accuracy.

cards.title: Squaring forgets a sign. The density must remember both.
cards.body: Let Y = X² for a continuous X. For y > 0, why is using only x = √y insufficient when X can be negative?
cards.answer:
Both √y and −√y map to y. Add their contributions:
fY(y) = [fX(√y) + fX(−√y)] / (2√y).

A change-of-variables formula must sum over all valid inverse branches; omit a branch and you can lose probability mass.
cards.takeaway: Count every preimage.

cards.title: Degrees of freedom count projected directions.
cards.body: For y ∼ N(μ,σ²I) and an orthogonal projector P of rank r, what is (y−μ)ᵀP(y−μ)/σ² distributed as?
cards.answer:
A chi-squared variable with r degrees of freedom. In an orthonormal coordinate system adapted to the projection, it is the sum of squares of r independent standard normals.

Mutually orthogonal projected Gaussian components produce independent quadratic forms. Gaussianity is essential to this exact distributional statement.
cards.takeaway: Rank becomes degrees of freedom.

cards.title: A residual can hide a large error in one direction.
cards.body: A=diag(1,10⁻⁸), b=(1,10⁻⁸)ᵀ, and x̂=(1,0)ᵀ. Find the true solution and residual.
cards.answer: The true solution is x=(1,1)ᵀ, so the error norm is 1. But r=b−Ax̂=(0,10⁻⁸)ᵀ is tiny. The small second singular value suppresses the visible residual while permitting a large error in x₂.
cards.takeaway: Weakly scaled directions can conceal solution error.

cards.title: Two inverse branches produce one density.
cards.body: X is uniform on [−1,1] and Y=X². Find F_Y(y) and f_Y(y) for 0<y<1.
cards.answer: F_Y(y)=P(−√y≤X≤√y)=√y. Differentiating gives f_Y(y)=1/(2√y). Both roots contribute in the change-of-variables formula. The density diverges near zero but integrates to one.
cards.takeaway: An unbounded density can still be integrable.

cards.title: A rank-two projection keeps two squared normals.
cards.body: Z∼N(0,I₃) and P=diag(1,1,0). Find the distribution, mean, and variance of ZᵀPZ.
cards.answer: It is Z₁²+Z₂²∼χ²₂, with mean 2 and variance 4. The third coordinate contributes nothing. Replacing P with a general symmetric matrix would usually give a weighted sum of chi-squared variables rather than this simple χ² result.
cards.takeaway: Idempotent eigenvalues make the chi-squared degrees simple.

cards.title: Exactly two solutions? Not for a linear system.
cards.body: Suppose Ax = b and Ay = b with x ≠ y. Can these be the only two solutions over the real numbers?
cards.answer:
No. For every real t, A[(1 − t)x + ty] = (1 − t)b + tb = b. The line through x and y contains infinitely many solutions.

Also A(y − x) = 0 with y − x nonzero, so the matrix has a nontrivial null space.
cards.takeaway: Two distinct solutions imply a whole affine line.

cards.title: Why does an envelope produce the right distribution?
cards.body: To sample normalized p using proposal q with p(x) ≤ Mq(x), draw X from q and accept with probability p(X)/(Mq(X)). What is the distribution conditional on acceptance?
cards.answer:
The joint accepted density is q(x) × p(x)/(Mq(x)) = p(x)/M. Integrating gives acceptance probability 1/M, so normalizing accepted draws gives p(x).

The envelope must bound the target everywhere; silently clipping a ratio above 1 can bias the result.
cards.takeaway: An envelope converts proposal draws into target draws.

cards.title: Why Gaussian fits and residuals are independent.
cards.body: Under y∼N(Xβ,σ²I), use H to show that Hy and (I−H)y are independent.
cards.answer: Their cross-covariance is σ²H(I−H)ᵀ=σ²(H−H²)=0. Both are linear transformations of the same Gaussian vector, hence jointly Gaussian. Zero cross-covariance then implies independence. Orthogonality alone is not a universal independence proof.
cards.takeaway: Geometry plus Gaussianity yields independence.

cards.title: The right-hand side must lie in the column space.
cards.answer: The first is consistent because the second equation is twice the first; it has infinitely many solutions x₁+2x₂=3. The second is inconsistent because it demands both twice that expression equal 6 and equal 7. Singularity alone does not decide existence.
cards.takeaway: A singular system can be consistent or inconsistent.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: A loose envelope wastes accepted opportunities.
cards.body: For normalized target p and proposal q with p≤Mq, suppose M=5. What fraction of proposals is accepted in ideal rejection sampling?
cards.answer: The acceptance probability is 1/M=0.2. On average, 5 proposals are needed per accepted draw. A smaller valid M improves efficiency; choosing M too small can invalidate the sampler rather than merely make it faster.
cards.takeaway: Tighten the envelope without breaking the bound.

cards.title: Extra fit compared with remaining noise.
cards.body: Nested Gaussian linear models have ranks p₀ < p₁ and residual sums SSE₀ and SSE₁. What F statistic tests the smaller model?
cards.answer:
F = [(SSE₀−SSE₁)/(p₁−p₀)] / [SSE₁/(n−p₁)]. Under the null and the spherical Gaussian error model, it has F(p₁−p₀, n−p₁) distribution.

The numerator measures improvement per added direction; the denominator estimates noise variance from the larger model.
cards.takeaway: Improvement per degree of freedom, scaled by noise.

cards.title: More unknowns do not guarantee a solution.
cards.body: A has fewer rows than columns. Is Ax=b necessarily solvable for every b?
cards.answer: No. Solvability for every b requires full row rank. For example, A=[[1,0,0],[0,0,0]] cannot produce b=(0,1)ᵀ. If a solution exists for an underdetermined real system, the nontrivial null space makes it nonunique.
cards.takeaway: Count equations and check rank.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: Rejection sampling can use an unnormalized target too.
cards.body: If f is an unnormalized target and f(x)≤cq(x), how do you accept, and what is the overall acceptance probability?
cards.answer: Accept a q draw with probability f(x)/(cq(x)). Accepted points have density f/Z where Z=∫f. The overall acceptance probability is Z/c, not automatically 1/c unless f is normalized. You need a valid envelope even when Z is unknown.
cards.takeaway: Keep track of which density is normalized.

cards.title: The central F law belongs to the null model.
cards.body: Why does the usual central F distribution for a nested-model test require the smaller model to contain the true mean?
cards.answer: Under the null, (H₁−H₀)μ=0, so the improvement quadratic form is centered and has a central chi-squared distribution. Under an alternative within the full model, it is generally noncentral. The test compares observed improvement with the null reference.
cards.takeaway: Centering the numerator uses the null hypothesis.

cards.title: Partial and complete pivoting search different places.
cards.body: Where do partial and complete pivoting choose the next pivot? Why can complete pivoting reorder the unknowns?
cards.answer:
Partial pivoting searches the active column and swaps rows. Complete pivoting searches the entire remaining submatrix and may swap both rows and columns. Row swaps reorder equations; column swaps reorder variables.

Track the column permutation when recovering the original ordering of the solution.
cards.takeaway: Rows reorder equations. Columns reorder unknowns.

cards.title: Change where you sample. Correct what you average.
cards.body: You need Eₚ[f(X)] but draw Xᵢ from q. What weights recover the expectation, and what support condition is essential?
cards.answer:
Use N⁻¹ Σ f(Xᵢ)p(Xᵢ)/q(Xᵢ). The identity follows from writing ∫fp = ∫(fp/q)q. Require q > 0 wherever fp contributes, and appropriate integrability for the expectation.

A poor q can produce enormous or infinite variance despite the identity being correct.
cards.takeaway: Support first. Variance second.

cards.title: One named factor can add several test degrees of freedom.
cards.body: A full model adds a four-level categorical factor to a smaller model. If all three added contrast directions are independent, how many numerator degrees of freedom does the joint F test use?
cards.answer: Three, because a four-level factor contributes three independent directions with an intercept. The count is rank(full)−rank(reduced), not the number of variable names added. Dependencies or empty levels can change that rank difference.
cards.takeaway: A factor is not necessarily a one-degree-of-freedom term.

cards.title: Find the first pivot under three policies.
cards.body: For A=[[1,9,2],[4,3,0],[−7,2,5]], which first pivot is selected with no pivoting, partial pivoting, and complete pivoting?
cards.answer: No pivoting uses 1. Partial pivoting searches the first column and selects −7 by magnitude. Complete pivoting searches the whole matrix and selects 9. Complete pivoting moves that entry into place with a column exchange here.
cards.takeaway: Compare magnitudes inside the correct search region.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: Weights correct an intentionally different sampling distribution.
cards.body: Target probabilities are p(A)=0.8,p(B)=0.2, but proposal probabilities are q(A)=q(B)=0.5. Give the weights for estimating Pₚ(A).
cards.answer: Weights p/q are 1.6 at A and 0.4 at B. The integrand is the indicator of A, so the ordinary estimator averages 1.6 for A draws and 0 for B draws. Its expectation under q is 0.5·1.6=0.8.
cards.takeaway: The weight corrects the probability of seeing each point.

cards.title: A bigger F means a smaller likelihood ratio.
cards.body: For nested Gaussian models fitted to the same n observations, express the maximized null/full likelihood ratio in terms of SSE₀ and SSE₁.
cards.answer: λ=(SSE₀/SSE₁)^(−n/2), assuming positive sums of squares. Since SSE₀/SSE₁=1+(p₁−p₀)F/(n−p₁), λ decreases as F grows. Small likelihood ratios and large F statistics express the same direction of evidence.
cards.takeaway: The two tests order the evidence the same way.

cards.title: One matrix. A hundred right-hand sides.
cards.body: You must solve Ax = b for many different b vectors. Why save an LU factorization instead of solving from scratch each time?
cards.answer:
For a dense n × n matrix, factorization costs O(n³), while two triangular solves cost O(n²) per right-hand side. Reuse the factors and permutation for each new b.

Explicitly forming A⁻¹ is usually unnecessary for applying the solve.
cards.takeaway: Factor once; solve many times.

cards.title: Weights cannot recover a region never sampled.
cards.body: If q(x)=0 on a region where f(x)p(x) has nonzero contribution, can importance weights fix the missing contribution?
cards.answer: No. No draw visits that region, and p/q is undefined there. The integral identity cannot represent the omitted mass through samples from q. Support coverage is a correctness requirement, separate from efficiency or variance.
cards.takeaway: You cannot reweight observations you can never obtain.

cards.title: Calculate the comparison before interpreting it.
cards.body: A reduced model has SSE=120 and rank 2. A full nested model has SSE=80 and rank 4, with n=24. Compute F and its null degrees of freedom.
cards.answer:
F = [(120−80)/(4−2)] / [80/(24−4)] = 20/4 = 5. The null reference is F(2,20), assuming the normal linear model conditions.

The number alone is not a p-value; compare it with that reference distribution.
cards.takeaway: Use ranks, not just the count of named predictors.

cards.title: Apply the row permutation to b too.
cards.body: Given PA=LU, list the steps to solve Ax=b without forming inverses.
cards.answer: First compute Pb. Solve Ly=Pb by forward substitution, then Ux=y by backward substitution. Applying P to A but not b changes the equations and generally gives the wrong solution.
cards.takeaway: The factorization transforms the whole system.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · repeated systems · companion practice

cards.title: Canceling a constant changes the estimator.
cards.body: With unnormalized importance weights wᵢ, why use Σwᵢf(Xᵢ)/Σwᵢ? Is it generally unbiased at finite N?
cards.answer:
The ratio cancels the unknown common scale in the target weights. It is generally biased at finite N because the denominator is random, though it is consistent under suitable conditions.

Ordinary importance sampling with a known normalized target has a different unbiasedness argument.
cards.takeaway: Self-normalization trades exact unbiasedness for convenience.

cards.title: An equality of two coefficients is one restriction.
cards.body: How would you express H₀: β₂ = β₃ in the form Λβ=c? Why can’t an arbitrary restriction always be tested when X is rank deficient?
cards.answer:
Choose a row Λ with 1 in position 2, −1 in position 3, and zeros elsewhere; set c=0.

For rank-deficient X, the tested linear functions must be estimable: each row of Λ must lie in C(Xᵀ), equivalently N(X) ⊆ N(Λ). Otherwise the restriction can change without changing the observable mean.
cards.takeaway: A testable claim must be identifiable from the model.

cards.title: Solve from the row with one unknown.
cards.answer: The first row gives x₁=2. The second gives 3·2+x₂=7, so x₂=1. The third gives 2−2+4x₃=12, so x₃=3. Forward substitution uses values as soon as they are known.
cards.takeaway: Lower triangular means solve top to bottom.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 exercises · triangular solves · companion practice

cards.title: A weighted average uses the weight sum, not the sample count.
cards.body: Unnormalized weights are (1,2,7) and function values are (0,1,1). Compute the self-normalized estimate.
cards.answer: (1·0+2·1+7·1)/(1+2+7)=9/10=0.9. Dividing by 3 would give 3, which is not a normalized average of these indicator values. This estimator differs from ordinary importance sampling with known normalized density weights.
cards.takeaway: Know which importance estimator you are implementing.

cards.title: Write two restrictions as two rows.
cards.body: For β=(β₀,β₁,β₂,β₃)ᵀ, express β₁=β₂ and β₃=2 as Λβ=c.
cards.answer: Use Λ=[[0,1,−1,0],[0,0,0,1]] and c=(0,2)ᵀ. The two rows are independent, so these are two independent restrictions. The nonzero right-hand side makes the restricted coefficient set affine rather than a subspace.
cards.takeaway: Each independent row encodes one restriction.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.48, printed p. 94

cards.title: The transpose reverses the factor order.
cards.body: If A=LU with nonsingular triangular factors, how do you solve Aᵀx=b using those same factors?
cards.answer: Aᵀ=UᵀLᵀ. First solve Uᵀy=b, then Lᵀx=y. Uᵀ is lower triangular; Lᵀ is upper triangular. A pivoted factorization requires handling the permutation as well.
cards.takeaway: Transpose the order as well as each factor.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.48, printed p. 94 · companion practice

cards.title: A thousand proposals can collapse to one influential point.
cards.body: In self-normalized importance sampling, one normalized weight is 0.99. Why should you be cautious about the estimate?
cards.answer: Almost the entire estimate is determined by one draw; the remaining samples contribute little. This suggests poor overlap or a heavy-tail mismatch between proposal and weighted target. More nominal samples alone may not reliably fix a bad proposal. Inspect weight concentration and relevant tail behavior.
cards.takeaway: Nominal sample size can hide weight concentration.

cards.title: Solve the normal equations and constraints together.
cards.body: For full-rank X, how can a block linear system compute constrained least squares under Λβ=c?
cards.answer: Solve [[XᵀX,Λᵀ],[Λ,0]] [β,ξ]ᵀ = [Xᵀy,c]ᵀ, with an appropriate scaling absorbed in multiplier ξ. The lower block enforces the constraints; the upper block imposes stationarity of the constrained objective.
cards.takeaway: Lagrange multipliers add equations for the restrictions.

sources.locator: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.44–46, printed p. 94

cards.title: You need A⁻¹Bc, not A⁻¹.
cards.body: For dense n×n A and B and vector c, how would you compute A⁻¹Bc efficiently?
cards.answer: Compute v=Bc, then solve Ax=v using a factorization of A. There is no need to form either A⁻¹ or the n×n product A⁻¹B. If A’s factors are already available, both the matrix-vector multiply and solve cost O(n²).
cards.takeaway: Apply the operator to the vector directly.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review Q2.44–46, printed p. 94 · companion practice

cards.title: Ten thousand chain states are not ten thousand independent draws.
cards.body: Why is the usual independent-sample standard error s/√N potentially too optimistic for positively autocorrelated MCMC samples?
cards.answer:
The variance of an average includes covariance terms between draws. Positive serial correlations add variance. Under suitable stationary mixing conditions, an effective sample size accounts for the integrated autocorrelation of the quantity being estimated.

The relevant correlation is for f(X), so different estimated quantities may have different effective sample sizes.
cards.takeaway: Dependence reduces the information in repeated draws.

cards.title: Don’t drop the estimated noise scale.
cards.body: For full-rank Gaussian regression, give the estimated standard error and t interval for βⱼ. Let s² = SSE/(n−p).
cards.answer:
The estimated standard error is s√[(XᵀX)⁻¹ⱼⱼ]. A pointwise interval is β̂ⱼ ± t₁₋α/₂,ₙ₋ₚ × s√[(XᵀX)⁻¹ⱼⱼ].

The square root of the matrix diagonal alone is missing the noise scale s. The t distribution accounts for estimating σ.
cards.takeaway: Coefficient uncertainty includes the noise scale.

cards.title: Symmetry alone does not buy you Cholesky.
cards.body: What extra condition makes a real symmetric matrix admit A = LLᵀ with a real, positive diagonal L?
cards.answer:
Positive definiteness. For A = [[4,2],[2,2]], L = [[2,0],[1,1]], and multiplying LLᵀ recovers A.

An SPD matrix can still be ill-conditioned—for example diag(1, 10⁻¹²). Existence of a convenient factorization does not guarantee low sensitivity.
cards.takeaway: Symmetric positive definite is the key condition.

cards.title: Strong correlation shrinks effective information.
cards.body: For a stationary quantity with autocorrelation ρₖ=rᵏ and r=0.8, use N_eff≈N/(1+2Σρₖ). What is N_eff for N=9000?
cards.answer: Σₖ≥1rᵏ=r/(1−r)=4. The integrated factor is 1+2·4=9, giving N_eff≈1000. This calculation assumes the stationary correlation model and a suitable central-limit regime; it does not account for failure to explore other modes.
cards.takeaway: An ESS estimate is conditional on the chain’s behavior.
cards.source: Lecture 03 · p. 6 and pp. 30–32 · comparison · companion practice

cards.title: A matrix entry is a variance multiplier.
cards.body: s²=9 and (XᵀX)⁻¹ⱼⱼ=0.04. What is the estimated standard error of β̂ⱼ? If β̂ⱼ=1.2, what t statistic tests βⱼ=0?
cards.answer: s=3 and √0.04=0.2, so SE=0.6. The t statistic is 1.2/0.6=2. Its reference degrees of freedom are n−p under the full-rank Gaussian model. The t value alone is not enough to determine the exact p-value without the degrees of freedom.
cards.takeaway: Take the square root of the complete variance expression.

cards.title: Positive diagonal entries alone are not enough.
cards.body: Does A=[[1,2],[2,1]] have a real Cholesky factor with positive diagonal?
cards.answer: No. It is symmetric with positive diagonal, but its eigenvalues are 3 and −1. Also v=(1,−1) gives vᵀAv=−2. It is not positive definite. Standard positive-definite Cholesky fails; symmetric-indefinite factorizations are a different method.
cards.takeaway: Positive definiteness concerns all directions.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review, printed pp. 92–96 · companion practice

cards.title: Count events or wait for one?
cards.body: Events arrive at constant rate ν. What are the distribution of the count by time t and the probability of no events?
cards.answer: N(t) ∼ Poisson(νt), so P(N(t) = 0) = exp(−νt) and E[N(t)] = νt. The time until the first event has survival function exp(−νt), hence an exponential distribution with rate ν.
cards.takeaway: Poisson counts and exponential waits are two views.

cards.title: A frequentist confidence interval describes a procedure.
cards.body: In the fixed-parameter frequentist model, what does 95% confidence mean for an interval-building method?
cards.answer: Across repeated datasets generated under the assumed model, about 95% of intervals produced by the method cover the fixed true parameter. It is not, by itself, a posterior probability statement about the parameter inside this particular realized interval.
cards.takeaway: Distinguish repeated-sampling coverage from posterior probability.

cards.title: A full-looking matrix can cost only linear work.
cards.body: If A = uvᵀ is n × n, how do you compute Ax without forming all n² entries?
cards.answer: Compute the scalar s = vᵀx, then return us. This takes O(n) arithmetic and stores two length-n vectors. A sum of k such terms costs O(nk), making low-rank structure valuable when k is small.
cards.takeaway: Use factors instead of expanding the matrix.

cards.title: Convert the rate into the interval’s expected count.
cards.body: A Poisson process has rate 2 per minute. Over 30 seconds, what are the expected count and probability of no events?
cards.answer: Thirty seconds is half a minute, so λt=1. The expected count is 1 and P(N=0)=e⁻¹≈0.3679. Always express time and rate in compatible units.
cards.takeaway: The Poisson parameter is rate times duration.

cards.title: Predicting one response is harder than estimating its mean.
cards.body: Why is a prediction interval for a new independent response wider than a confidence interval for its conditional mean at the same x₀?
cards.answer:
The mean estimate has variance σ²x₀(XᵀX)⁻¹x₀ᵀ. Predicting a new response adds its independent noise variance σ², giving σ²[1+x₀(XᵀX)⁻¹x₀ᵀ].

Under the Gaussian model, replace σ by s and use the appropriate t quantile. The added 1 is the future observation’s uncertainty.
cards.takeaway: A future observation adds its own noise.

cards.title: All columns point in one direction.
cards.body: For nonzero u and v, why does uvᵀ have rank one?
cards.answer: Column j equals vⱼu, so every column lies in span(u). At least one column is nonzero because v is nonzero, so the column space has dimension exactly one. If either vector is zero, the rank is zero.
cards.takeaway: An outer product has one column-space direction.
cards.source: Heath · Ch. 2 review · rank-one matrices · companion practice

cards.title: Nonoverlapping intervals carry independent counts.
cards.body: For a homogeneous Poisson process, how are counts in [0,1] and (1,2] related? How about N(1) and N(2)?
cards.answer: Counts in disjoint time intervals are independent. But N(2)=N(1)+the second-interval count, so cumulative counts N(1) and N(2) are dependent. Do not confuse independent increments with independent cumulative values.
cards.takeaway: Independence belongs to increments, not the accumulated count.

cards.title: The extra noise is visible in the formula.
cards.body: Let s=2 and x₀(XᵀX)⁻¹x₀ᵀ=0.25. Compare the estimated standard deviations used for a mean-response interval and a new-observation interval.
cards.answer: For the estimated mean, s√0.25=1. For a new independent observation, s√(1+0.25)=√5≈2.236. Using the same t multiplier therefore yields a wider prediction interval.
cards.takeaway: The prediction standard deviation includes the added one.

cards.title: The normal equations can square your trouble.
cards.body: For full-column-rank X, how does κ₂(XᵀX) compare with κ₂(X)? Why might a least-squares solver use QR or SVD?
cards.answer:
The eigenvalues of XᵀX are the squared singular values of X, so κ₂(XᵀX) = κ₂(X)². Explicitly forming XᵀX can worsen numerical sensitivity.

QR or SVD avoids that particular formation and is generally preferable for difficult least-squares problems. They cannot remove intrinsic ill-conditioning in the data.
cards.takeaway: A correct formula need not be the best algorithm.

cards.title: Remember which geometric convention you are using.
cards.body: An event succeeds independently each generation with probability p. T counts generations including the successful one. What are P(T=t) and E[T]?
cards.answer:
For t = 1,2,…, P(T=t) = (1−p)ᵗ⁻¹p and E[T] = 1/p. The t−1 failures happen before the success.

If instead T counts failures before success, its support starts at zero and its mean is (1−p)/p.
cards.takeaway: Define the support before using the formula.

cards.title: 95% each does not mean 95% all at once.
cards.body: Why can many pointwise 95% confidence intervals fail to provide 95% simultaneous coverage?
cards.answer:
Each interval controls its own marginal coverage. The event that all intervals cover is a different event, typically with lower probability.

Scheffé’s approach uses a confidence ellipsoid to produce wider intervals that jointly cover all linear combinations under the normal model. Pointwise and simultaneous procedures answer different coverage questions.
cards.takeaway: State which collection of claims is covered.

cards.title: An orthogonal change leaves the residual length unchanged.
cards.body: For full-column-rank X with reduced QR factorization X=QR, how do you solve minβ ‖y−Xβ‖²?
cards.answer: Split y into QQᵀy and (I−QQᵀ)y. Then ‖y−QRβ‖²=‖Qᵀy−Rβ‖²+‖(I−QQᵀ)y‖². The second term is independent of β. Solve the triangular system Rβ=Qᵀy.
cards.takeaway: Rotate the least-squares problem into a triangular solve.
cards.source: Heath · §3.3–3.5 · supporting least-squares reading · companion practice

cards.title: Surviving five failures is a tail event.
cards.body: T counts trials through the first success with probability p=0.2 each trial. Find P(T>5) and P(T=3).
cards.answer: P(T>5)=0.8⁵=0.32768. P(T=3)=0.8²·0.2=0.128. The first event asks for five failures; the second asks for two failures followed by success.
cards.takeaway: A tail probability and a point probability use different events.

cards.title: Scheffé protects a whole family of linear combinations.
cards.body: In the full-rank Gaussian model, what multiplier replaces the pointwise t critical value for simultaneous Scheffé intervals over all linear combinations of β?
cards.answer: Use √[p F₁₋α;p,n−p] in aᵀβ̂ ± s√[pF]√[aᵀ(XᵀX)⁻¹a]. The larger family of protected statements costs wider intervals. For a lower-dimensional prespecified family, the appropriate dimension can differ.
cards.takeaway: The protection family determines the multiplier.

cards.title: A pseudoinverse chooses among equivalent fits.
cards.body: When X is rank deficient, what extra criterion selects the Moore–Penrose least-squares solution X⁺y?
cards.answer: It has minimum Euclidean coefficient norm among all least-squares solutions. Other solutions add vectors in N(X), leaving fitted values unchanged but increasing norm relative to the minimum-norm solution. Numerical pseudoinverses also need a tolerance for deciding which singular values count as zero.
cards.takeaway: Minimum residual and minimum coefficient norm are separate criteria.
cards.source: Heath · §3.3–3.5 · supporting least-squares reading · companion practice

cards.title: One sibling among the other offspring.
cards.body: In the homework reproduction scheme, each of N parents has exactly two offspring. Two survivors are sampled uniformly without replacement. What is their probability of sharing a parent one generation back?
cards.answer:
Given one sampled offspring, exactly one of the remaining 2N−1 offspring is its sibling. The probability is 1/(2N−1).

For large N it is approximately 1/(2N). The exact answer depends on the stated reproduction scheme; do not automatically substitute a different population model’s formula.
cards.takeaway: Model details determine the transition probability.

cards.title: Bigger space. Smaller orthogonal complement.
cards.body: If A ⊆ B are subspaces, why is B⊥ ⊆ A⊥?
cards.answer:
A vector perpendicular to every vector of B is automatically perpendicular to every vector of its subset A. So it belongs to A⊥.

In finite dimensions, taking complements twice returns the original subspace. This is useful for proving (W₁∩W₂)⊥ = W₁⊥ + W₂⊥.
cards.takeaway: Orthogonal complements reverse inclusion.

cards.title: Check the exact finite-N probability before taking a limit.
cards.body: Under the homework’s two-offspring-per-parent scheme with N=3 parents, what is the one-generation probability that two distinct sampled offspring share a parent?
cards.answer: There are 6 offspring. Given the first, exactly 1 of the other 5 is its sibling, so the probability is 1/5. The approximation 1/(2N)=1/6 is not exact at this small N.
cards.takeaway: Asymptotic approximations need a scale check.

cards.title: A sum of perpendicular pieces annihilates an intersection.
cards.body: If v=v₁+v₂ with v₁∈W₁⊥ and v₂∈W₂⊥, why is v∈(W₁∩W₂)⊥?
cards.answer: For every w in the intersection, w belongs to both spaces. Thus vᵀw=v₁ᵀw+v₂ᵀw=0+0=0. This proves one inclusion in (W₁∩W₂)⊥=W₁⊥+W₂⊥; the reverse needs its own argument.
cards.takeaway: A set equality requires both inclusions.

cards.title: A waiting-time limit needs the right clock.
cards.body: Let T be geometric with success probability about 1/(2N). As N grows, why examine T/(2N) instead of T itself?
cards.answer:
The mean waiting time grows like 2N. For t ≥ 0, P(T/(2N) > t) is approximately (1−1/(2N))^(2Nt), which tends to e⁻ᵗ. Thus the scaled waiting time approaches Exp(1).

At a fixed unscaled time, the success probability tends to zero; rescaling reveals a nondegenerate limit.
cards.takeaway: Scale time with the growing mean.

cards.title: The perpendicular remainder must have zero length.
cards.body: In finite-dimensional Euclidean space, prove that (A⊥)⊥⊆A for a subspace A.
cards.answer: Decompose u∈(A⊥)⊥ as u=a+b with a∈A and b∈A⊥. Since u is perpendicular to b, 0=uᵀb=aᵀb+bᵀb=‖b‖². Therefore b=0 and u=a∈A. The other inclusion follows directly from orthogonality.
cards.takeaway: Use the orthogonal decomposition to prove membership.

cards.title: Two branches, twice the rate.
cards.body: Two independent lineages each accumulate mutations at rate ν for a fixed time t. What is the distribution of their total mutation count? What if t is random?
cards.answer:
Conditional on t, the independent Poisson counts add to Poisson(2νt). If t is random, the unconditional count is a mixture over t, not generally Poisson with mean 2νE[t].

The law of total expectation still gives E[count] = 2νE[t].
cards.takeaway: Conditioning and averaging distributions are different steps.

cards.title: The transpose belongs on the other side.
cards.body: If Y has mean μ and covariance Σ, what are the mean and covariance of AY+b? Does this require Y to be Gaussian?
cards.answer:
Mean: Aμ+b. Covariance: AΣAᵀ. These hold for any random vector with finite second moments.

If Y is Gaussian, the transformed vector is also Gaussian; that is an additional distributional conclusion, not a prerequisite for the moment formulas.
cards.takeaway: Linear transformations act on both sides of covariance.

cards.title: Random exposure adds extra count variation.
cards.body: If K|T∼Poisson(2νT), use total variance to express Var(K), assuming the moments exist.
cards.answer: Var(K)=E[Var(K|T)]+Var(E[K|T])=2νE[T]+4ν²Var(T). Random exposure time contributes the second term. Unless T is constant, the marginal variance can exceed the mean, unlike an ordinary Poisson count.
cards.takeaway: Mixing a rate or exposure can create overdispersion.

cards.title: Zero covariance is not universal independence.
cards.body: Let X be standard normal and Y=X². Are X and Y independent just because Cov(X,Y)=0?
cards.answer: No. Symmetry gives E[X³]=0 and thus zero covariance, but Y is determined by X. Zero cross-covariance implies independence for jointly Gaussian blocks; (X,X²) is not jointly Gaussian.
cards.takeaway: Check joint normality, not just marginal facts.

cards.title: Invert one line segment at a time.
cards.body: A CDF is linear between (xᵢ,Fᵢ) and (xᵢ₊₁,Fᵢ₊₁), with Fᵢ₊₁ > Fᵢ. Given uniform U in this CDF interval, how do you produce X?
cards.answer:
X = xᵢ + (U−Fᵢ)(xᵢ₊₁−xᵢ)/(Fᵢ₊₁−Fᵢ). First locate the segment in CDF space, then interpolate in x. Flat segments have zero probability and should not cause division by zero.

The density on a segment is its CDF slope.
cards.takeaway: Find the probability interval, then invert.

cards.title: Small pairwise correlations do not rule out a dependency.
cards.body: Why can pairwise predictor correlations miss multicollinearity?
cards.answer:
A predictor can be nearly a linear combination of several others without being almost perfectly correlated with any one of them. Examine the design as a whole, using appropriate scaling, singular values, or regressions of individual predictors on the remaining set.

Near-collinearity inflates uncertainty in certain coefficient directions even when fitted values are relatively stable.
cards.takeaway: Dependencies can involve more than two columns.

cards.title: Interpolate in probability coordinates.
cards.body: A linear CDF segment joins (x,F)=(2,0.3) and (5,0.9). For U=0.5, find the inverse sample.
cards.answer: X=2+[(0.5−0.3)/(0.9−0.3)](5−2)=2+(1/3)·3=3. The fraction is measured along the CDF range, then applied to the x interval.
cards.takeaway: Probability fraction maps to position fraction.

cards.title: Two uncertain slopes can still make a stable prediction.
cards.body: Why can two nearly duplicate predictors give unstable individual coefficients but fairly stable fitted values on the observed data?
cards.answer: Changing one coefficient upward and the other downward can nearly cancel in Xβ because the columns are close. The weakly determined difference direction may have high coefficient variance, while the well-determined sum direction governs most observed predictions. Extrapolation away from the observed relationship can expose the uncertainty.
cards.takeaway: Ask which coefficient combination the data actually constrain.

cards.title: A flat CDF interval contains no probability mass.
cards.body: A CDF is constant on x∈[2,4]. Should an inverse sampler choose points uniformly throughout [2,4] whenever it encounters that CDF value?
cards.answer: No. A flat segment has zero probability mass, so a continuous uniform U hits that single CDF value with probability zero. A robust generalized inverse handles the boundary convention without dividing by a zero CDF increment.
cards.takeaway: Flat in the CDF means absent mass, not uniform density.

cards.title: A predictor is almost predicted by the other predictors.
cards.body: Regressing predictor xⱼ on the other predictors gives Rⱼ²=0.95. What is its VIF, and what does it describe?
cards.answer:
VIFⱼ = 1/(1−Rⱼ²) = 20. In the standard regression setting, it quantifies coefficient-variance inflation associated with linear dependence on the other predictors.

A large VIF is a diagnostic, not an automatic command to delete a substantively important variable.
cards.takeaway: Explain the redundancy before changing the model.

cards.title: A radius and an angle make two Gaussians.
cards.body: For independent uniform U₁,U₂ in (0,1), define R = √(−2 log U₁), Θ = 2πU₂. Why do R cos Θ and R sin Θ become independent standard normals?
cards.answer: R has density r exp(−r²/2) for r ≥ 0, while Θ is independent uniform on [0,2π). The polar-to-Cartesian inverse Jacobian contributes 1/r. Their joint density becomes exp(−(x²+y²)/2)/(2π), which factors into two standard normal densities.
cards.takeaway: The Jacobian cancels the radial factor.

cards.title: Variance inflation and standard-error inflation differ.
cards.body: A predictor has VIF=9. Holding the comparison’s noise and predictor sum of squares fixed, by what factor is its standard error inflated?
cards.answer: By √9=3, because VIF multiplies the coefficient variance. Confusing variance with standard deviation would overstate the standard-error factor as 9.
cards.takeaway: Square roots convert variance factors to error-bar factors.

cards.title: Derive the radial distribution before the Cartesian one.
cards.body: For R=√(−2 log U), U uniform on (0,1), compute P(R≤r) for r≥0.
cards.answer: R≤r is equivalent to −2log U≤r², hence U≥exp(−r²/2). Therefore F_R(r)=1−exp(−r²/2), and f_R(r)=r exp(−r²/2). For r<0 the CDF is zero. Be careful: solving for U reverses the inequality.
cards.takeaway: Track the monotonicity of each transformation.

cards.title: Read the exponent in the generalized VIF output.
cards.body: Software prints GVIF^(1/(2·df))=2 for a factor. What is GVIF^(1/df), the corresponding variance-inflation scale used in your notes?
cards.answer: Square the displayed value: 4. The displayed root is on a standard-error-like scale, while squaring returns the variance-inflation scale. Do not compare differently exponentiated columns with the same numerical cutoff.
cards.takeaway: A diagnostic threshold must match the reported scale.

cards.title: The square of the Gaussian radius is exponential up to scale.
cards.body: In Box–Muller, what is the distribution of R²/2?
cards.answer: R²/2=−log U, so it has an Exp(1) distribution. Equivalently, R² has χ²₂ distribution because it equals the sum of squares of two independent standard normals. This links inverse transforms, polar geometry, and chi-squared laws.
cards.takeaway: One construction can reveal several distribution identities.

cards.title: Keep only what the earlier columns cannot explain.
cards.body: How does Gram–Schmidt construct the next orthogonal direction from xₖ?
cards.answer:
Subtract its projection onto the span of earlier columns: ũₖ=(I−Hₖ₋₁)xₖ. Normalize if an orthonormal basis is desired. A zero residual means the new column adds no direction.

The ordered partial spans are preserved, but the particular basis depends on the input ordering. Numerically stable variants matter in computation.
cards.takeaway: A new basis vector is a residual.

cards.title: The square-to-disk rejection rate is geometric.
cards.body: Draw a point uniformly from [−1,1]² and accept it when 0 < x²+y² < 1. What fraction is rejected?
cards.answer:
The square area is 4 and disk area is π, so acceptance probability is π/4 and rejection probability is 1−π/4 ≈ 0.2146. Removing the origin or boundary does not change the ideal continuous probability.

In the polar normal sampler, excluding zero also prevents a division by zero and log(0).
cards.takeaway: Area ratios become acceptance probabilities.

cards.title: Remove the first vector’s component.
cards.body: Take x₁=(1,1)ᵀ and x₂=(1,0)ᵀ. Compute x₂’s residual after projection onto x₁.
cards.answer: The projection coefficient is (x₁ᵀx₂)/(x₁ᵀx₁)=1/2. The residual is (1,0)−(1/2)(1,1)=(1/2,−1/2). Its dot product with x₁ is zero. Normalize it to obtain (1,−1)/√2.
cards.takeaway: Subtract the projection before normalizing.

cards.title: The accepted disk point can replace an angle calculation.
cards.body: With (V₁,V₂) uniform in the unit disk and S=V₁²+V₂²>0, what transformation gives a standard normal pair?
cards.answer: Set (X,Y)=√[−2log S/S]·(V₁,V₂). Under uniform disk sampling, S is uniform on (0,1) and independent of the angle. The transformed radius becomes √(−2log S), the same radius law used in Box–Muller.
cards.takeaway: Uniform squared radius supplies the inverse-transform input.

cards.title: Changing coordinates does not create information.
cards.body: You orthogonalize all predictors and obtain uncorrelated transformed coefficient estimates. Did you eliminate uncertainty in the original coefficients?
cards.answer:
No. If the transformation is invertible and all directions are retained, it is the same model in a new basis. Transforming coefficients and covariance back recovers the original OLS uncertainty.

Reducing uncertainty requires new information or a changed estimator/model, such as regularization or dropping directions—with corresponding tradeoffs.
cards.takeaway: An easier coordinate system is not new data.

cards.title: How many square proposals per accepted disk point?
cards.body: If independent proposals are accepted with probability π/4, what is the expected number of proposals for one accepted point?
cards.answer: The proposal count is geometric with mean 1/(π/4)=4/π≈1.273. This counts proposals, not necessarily runtime: vectorization, random-number generation, and function costs also matter when comparing normal samplers.
cards.takeaway: Acceptance probability predicts work only in proposal units.

cards.title: Large predictor variance need not mean useful signal.
cards.body: PCR keeps the leading principal components of X. Why can it discard a direction that matters for predicting y?
cards.answer:
PCA chooses directions using variation in X alone. A low-variance predictor direction can still be strongly associated with y. Dropping it may lose signal.

Keeping all components recovers OLS when X has full column rank; keeping fewer changes the model and generally introduces bias. Select component count using an appropriate evaluation design.
cards.takeaway: Predictor variance is not response relevance.

cards.title: To get there in two steps, sum over the middle.
cards.body: For a time-homogeneous discrete Markov chain with row-stochastic transition matrix P, what is the probability of going from i to k in two steps?
cards.answer:
(P²)ᵢₖ = Σⱼ PᵢⱼPⱼₖ. Multiply the probabilities along each possible two-step path and sum over intermediate states.

The continuous-state counterpart integrates over the intermediate state. This is the Chapman–Kolmogorov composition rule.
cards.takeaway: Compose paths by summing over intermediate states.

cards.title: Keeping all principal components is only a rotation.
cards.body: For a full-rank centered predictor matrix, why can PCR with all p components reproduce OLS while PCR with k
cards.answer: The full orthogonal component matrix is an invertible change of coordinates preserving C(X). Keeping only k components restricts the fitted-value space to C(XQ₁:ₖ). That removes directions and can reduce variance at the price of bias.
cards.takeaway: Truncation changes the model; rotation alone does not.

cards.title: Choose a row-vector or column-vector convention once.
cards.body: Rows of P index the current state and columns index the next state. How do you propagate a row distribution p? How about a column distribution?
cards.answer: For a row distribution, p_next=pP. For a column distribution, p_next=Pᵀp. Both express the same sum over incoming states. Mixing the conventions can produce plausible-looking but incorrect equations.
cards.takeaway: Transition orientation must match distribution orientation.

cards.title: Unsupervised does not mean safe outside validation.
cards.body: Why should PCA for a cross-validated PCR model be fitted inside each training fold even though it does not use y?
cards.answer: The validation predictors affect estimated means, scales, and component directions if PCA is fitted on the entire dataset. That lets held-out data shape the procedure being evaluated. Fit all learned transformations inside the fold to reproduce genuinely unseen-data use.
cards.takeaway: Preprocessing can leak information without reading labels.

cards.title: Count both routes into the destination.
cards.body: With P=[[0.8,0.2],[0.3,0.7]], compute the two-step probability A→B.
cards.answer: There are two paths: A→A→B contributes 0.8·0.2=0.16, and A→B→B contributes 0.2·0.7=0.14. The total is 0.30. This is entry (A,B) of P².
cards.takeaway: Sum products over intermediate states.

cards.title: PCR and PLS look for different directions.
cards.body: What information does PLS use when constructing components that ordinary PCA for PCR does not?
cards.answer:
PLS uses association with the response as well as predictor structure. PCA for PCR finds predictor-variance directions without considering y.

Neither method universally wins. When evaluating either, fit centering, scaling, and component construction inside each training fold, then compare held-out predictions.
cards.takeaway: Supervised components still need honest validation.

cards.title: Probability has an incoming and an outgoing budget.
cards.body: For a birth–death chain with upward rate w₊(n) and downward rate w₋(n), write the structure of dpₙ/dt.
cards.answer:
dpₙ/dt = w₊(n−1)pₙ₋₁ + w₋(n+1)pₙ₊₁ − [w₊(n)+w₋(n)]pₙ.

Incoming rates are evaluated at the source states n−1 and n+1, not at n. At boundaries, omit impossible transitions or define their rates to be zero.
cards.takeaway: Incoming flux minus outgoing flux.

cards.title: PLS components already use the response.
cards.body: What is especially problematic about fitting PLS components on all observations before splitting into training and validation sets?
cards.answer: PLS uses the response to construct its directions. Fitting it before the split allows validation outcomes to influence the feature representation. The later model evaluation is therefore contaminated even if the final regression fit uses only training rows.
cards.takeaway: Supervised feature construction belongs inside training.

cards.title: Every outgoing flux enters somewhere else.
cards.body: Why does summing a finite-state master equation over all states give total derivative zero, assuming all transitions remain in the state space?
cards.answer: Each term w(i,j)pⱼ enters state i and leaves state j. Summing all equations cancels these paired contributions. This preserves Σpᵢ=1 from a normalized initial condition. Missing boundary terms or incorrect rate indices can break conservation.
cards.takeaway: Conservation is a useful equation check.

cards.title: A pure-death process cannot leave zero.
cards.body: For n particles independently decaying at rate γ each, write dpₙ/dt and the n=0 equation.
cards.answer: dpₙ/dt=γ(n+1)pₙ₊₁−γnpₙ. At zero, dp₀/dt=γp₁: there is inflow from one particle and no outflow. A loss term involving a negative particle count would violate the model.
cards.takeaway: Boundary states need explicit impossible-transition rates.
cards.source: Lecture 04 · radioactive decay, pp. 61–63 · companion practice

cards.title: A generator turns jumps into change in an average.
cards.body: For jumps x → x + νⱼ at rates aⱼ(x), what does the generator do to a test function f?
cards.answer:
Lf(x) = Σⱼ aⱼ(x)[f(x+νⱼ) − f(x)]. Subject to the usual integrability conditions, dE[f(X)]/dt = E[Lf(X)].

Choosing f(x) = x yields mean dynamics; choosing products or squares produces moment equations. This avoids re-deriving every moment from the full probability equation.
cards.takeaway: Rate × change, summed over jumps.

cards.title: A constant observable cannot change.
cards.body: For Lf(x)=Σⱼaⱼ(x)[f(x+νⱼ)−f(x)], what is L1? Why is this a useful check?
cards.answer: L1=0 because every difference is 1−1=0. Consequently dE[1]/dt=0, reflecting conservation of total probability. A proposed generator that changes a constant has a missing or incorrect loss term.
cards.takeaway: Generators annihilate constant functions.

cards.title: Choose f(n)=n to get the mean equation.
cards.body: For pure death with rate γn and jump −1, use the generator to obtain the mean dynamics.
cards.answer: Lf(n)=γn[(n−1)−n]=−γn. Thus m′=E[Lf]=−γm, giving m(t)=m(0)e⁻ᵞᵗ. This closes exactly because the drift is linear. Individual trajectories remain discrete and random.
cards.takeaway: The mean equation can be exact without deterministic paths.
cards.source: Lecture 04 · radioactive decay mean · companion practice

cards.title: Which color must leave each urn?
cards.body: Each urn has N balls; B total are blue; n blue are in the left urn. Swaps occur at rate λ. What factors make the upward rate w₊(n)?
cards.answer:
To increase n, draw a green ball from the left, probability (N−n)/N, and a blue ball from the right, probability (B−n)/N. Thus w₊(n) = λ(N−n)(B−n)/N².

Similarly, w₋(n) = λn(N−B+n)/N². Swaps of equal colors do not change n.
cards.takeaway: Count the events that actually change the state.

cards.title: Check rates at the extreme states.
cards.body: For the homework urn model with 0≤n≤B≤N, evaluate w₋(0) and w₊(B). Why must these vanish?
cards.answer: w₋(0)=0 because the left urn has no blue ball to lose. w₊(B)=0 because the right urn has no blue ball to send. Nonzero outward rates would permit impossible negative or excessive blue counts.
cards.takeaway: Physical constraints should appear in the rates.

cards.title: Quadratic rates can leave a linear drift.
cards.body: Using the urn rates, w₊(n)−w₋(n) = λ(B−2n)/N. Why does the equation for the mean close exactly?
cards.answer:
The drift is linear, so its expectation depends only on m = E[n]: m′ = (λ/N)(B−2m). Therefore m(t) = B/2 + (m(0)−B/2)exp(−2λt/N).

The relaxation timescale is N/(2λ). The limiting mean is approached asymptotically, not reached exactly at a finite time in general.
cards.takeaway: Closure depends on the drift, not each rate alone.

cards.title: A relaxation time removes one factor of e.
cards.body: For N=50, λ=1 per second, B=50, and n(0)=50, what is the exact mean at t=25 seconds?
cards.answer: m(t)=25+25exp(−2t/50). At t=25, m=25+25/e≈34.197. The relaxation time N/(2λ)=25 seconds shrinks the deviation from equilibrium by 1/e, not all the way to zero.
cards.takeaway: A timescale is not a finite equilibration deadline.

cards.title: At equilibrium, the left urn is a sample without replacement.
cards.body: Why is the stationary blue-ball count hypergeometric rather than binomial?
cards.answer:
The left urn contains N of the total 2N balls, with exactly B blue in the whole system. The count has probability C(B,n)C(2N−B,N−n)/C(2N,N). Fixed total counts couple the draws; they are not independent Bernoulli trials.

Checking πₙw₊(n) = πₙ₊₁w₋(n+1) verifies detailed balance.
cards.takeaway: A conserved finite population suggests hypergeometric counts.

cards.title: Count a small urn system by hand.
cards.body: Two urns each contain N=2 balls, with B=2 blue in total. Under uniform equilibrium allocation, find P(n=0),P(n=1),P(n=2) for the left urn.
cards.answer: There are C(4,2)=6 equally likely two-ball subsets. Counts are C(2,n)C(2,2−n): 1,4,1. Thus probabilities are (1/6,2/3,1/6), with mean 1. This gives a small exact target for testing a simulation.
cards.takeaway: Small state spaces make good validation cases.

cards.title: Detailed balance gives a stationary recursion.
cards.body: For neighboring states of a birth–death chain, how can you build stationary probabilities recursively from the rates?
cards.answer: Use πₙ₊₁/πₙ=w₊(n)/w₋(n+1) wherever the denominator is positive. Starting from an arbitrary scale π₀, multiply these ratios, then normalize. Check boundaries and whether the resulting sum is finite.
cards.takeaway: Compute relative weights first, normalization last.

cards.title: An event histogram can overweight busy states.
cards.body: You simulate a continuous-time chain and count its state once per jump. Does that histogram necessarily estimate the fraction of time spent in each state?
cards.answer:
No. States with faster exit rates generate more events per unit time. Estimate time occupancy by weighting each visited state by its holding time, or sample the trajectory at equally spaced times.

An event-index histogram describes the embedded jump chain, which can have a different stationary distribution.
cards.takeaway: Weight by time when estimating time occupancy.

cards.title: Two visits can occupy very different fractions of time.
cards.body: A trajectory visits A for 9 seconds and B for 1 second. Compare its per-visit histogram with its time-occupancy histogram.
cards.answer: The per-visit histogram assigns 1/2 to each because there are two visits. Time occupancy assigns 0.9 to A and 0.1 to B. If the question concerns the stationary state at a randomly chosen time, the latter is the relevant estimate.
cards.takeaway: Match the histogram weights to the sampling question.
cards.source: HW2 · Q3(e) · simulation diagnostic · companion practice

cards.title: One reaction changes several counts at once.
cards.body: For grass consumption G + R → 2R, what is the change vector in (G,R,F)? What is the change for R + F → 2F?
cards.answer:
Grass consumption changes counts by (−1,+1,0). Predation changes them by (0,−1,+1). Multiply each change vector by its propensity to build the drift, then sum over reactions.

Rates describe how often an event occurs; change vectors describe what each event does.
cards.takeaway: Separate event frequency from event effect.

cards.title: A death reaction contributes a negative drift.
cards.body: For rabbits born through G+R→2R at propensity βGR/N, dying at μR, and eaten at γRF/N, write the exact equation for dE[R]/dt.
cards.answer: dE[R]/dt=(β/N)E[GR]−μE[R]−(γ/N)E[RF]. The birth jump adds one rabbit and the two loss channels each remove one. Replacing product moments with products of means is an additional closure step.
cards.takeaway: Write the exact moment equation before approximating it.

cards.title: From event counts to population densities.
cards.body: Use g=G/N, r=R/N, f=F/N for the grass–rabbit–fox model. What are the mean-field density equations?
cards.answer:
g′ = α(1−g) − βgr
r′ = βgr − μr − γrf
f′ = γrf − δf.

This deterministic closure neglects correlations in the stochastic counts. At a coexistence fixed point r* = δ/γ, g* = α/(α+βδ/γ), and f* = (βg*−μ)/γ must be positive.
cards.takeaway: Track gains and losses before solving fixed points.

cards.title: A positive fixed point must satisfy positivity, not just zero derivatives.
cards.body: For the grass–rabbit–fox mean-field system, use f*>0 to derive r*, then state the condition for f*>0.
cards.answer: From f′=f(γr−δ), coexistence gives r*=δ/γ. Then g*=α/(α+βδ/γ) and f*=(βg*−μ)/γ. Coexistence requires positive parameters and β α/(α+βδ/γ)>μ. Algebraic fixed points outside nonnegative densities are not biologically admissible.
cards.takeaway: Solve equilibrium equations and check the state constraints.

cards.title: Half a fox cannot keep a population alive.
cards.body: Why can an SSA realization go extinct when the mean-field ODE shows small positive densities?
cards.answer:
SSA uses integer populations and discrete events. A last individual can disappear, after which an absorbing boundary may prevent recovery. A smooth ODE describes continuous densities and generally misses that event-level extinction mechanism.

Larger system size often reduces typical relative fluctuations, but rare events and boundary behavior still deserve separate analysis.
cards.takeaway: Small counts expose the discreteness.

cards.title: The next reaction can be in any cell.
cards.body: In a Delta–Notch grid, should you independently advance each cell by one full SSA event and call that one shared time step?
cards.answer:
No. For a direct SSA of the coupled system, enumerate all allowed reaction channels across all cells, sum their propensities, sample one global waiting time, and choose one channel in proportion to its propensity. Then update any affected neighboring propensities.

Enforce the count bounds and the specified boundary cells; they are part of the model.
cards.takeaway: Coupled cells share one event clock.

cards.title: Boundary cells contribute to the specified neighborhood.
cards.body: In the Delta–Notch model, what details must a correct computation of neighboring mean Delta respect?
cards.answer: Exclude the focal cell itself; use the specified hexagonal-neighbor offsets; and implement the stated fictitious boundary cells with Delta fixed at zero. Replacing the boundary by periodic wrapping or averaging only over existing interior neighbors defines a different model.
cards.takeaway: Neighborhood and boundary rules are part of the dynamics.

cards.title: Clip the event rate before an impossible jump, not the state afterward.
cards.body: The model limits molecule counts to [0,Z]. Why is setting a production propensity to zero at Z preferable to letting the event occur and clipping the resulting state?
cards.answer: The specification makes that transition impossible. A zero propensity removes it from both the channel selection and total event rate. Sampling a forbidden event and clipping afterward can waste event time and alter the state process unless treated by a separately justified null-event method.
cards.takeaway: Forbidden channels should not silently change the clock.

cards.title: A bigger step can make a negative population.
cards.body: Tau-leaping draws Poisson reaction counts over a time interval τ. What assumption makes this useful, and what can go wrong?
cards.answer:
It approximates propensities as constant over the interval, using counts Kⱼ ∼ Poisson(aⱼτ). Large changes can violate that approximation, and unbounded Poisson draws may consume more molecules than exist.

Control the step or use a method with appropriate population constraints; merely accepting negative counts produces an invalid state.
cards.takeaway: Speed comes with an approximation to control.

cards.title: A propensity becomes an expected count over a step.
cards.body: For constant propensity a=12 per second and τ=0.1 seconds, what is the tau-leap reaction-count distribution and its mean?
cards.answer: K∼Poisson(aτ)=Poisson(1.2), with mean and variance 1.2. K need not be 0 or 1; that is how a leap can skip individual-event simulation. The approximation needs propensities to remain nearly constant over the interval.
cards.takeaway: Rate times duration sets the count parameter.

cards.title: An exponential rate is events divided by total waiting time.
cards.body: Given N independent exponential waiting times tᵢ with rate ν, derive the maximum-likelihood estimate.
cards.answer:
The log likelihood is N log ν − νΣtᵢ. Its derivative is N/ν − Σtᵢ, giving ν̂ = N/Σtᵢ = 1/mean(t), when total time is positive.

This identifies a point estimate; uncertainty in ν still needs to be quantified.
cards.takeaway: Use the likelihood of the observations themselves.

cards.title: Add waiting times before estimating a common rate.
cards.body: You observe waiting times 0.2,0.3,0.5 seconds from independent Exp(ν) draws. What is the MLE of ν?
cards.answer: N=3 and the total waiting time is 1 second, so ν̂=3 per second. The estimate is reciprocal of the sample mean, not the average of the reciprocals of the individual times.
cards.takeaway: Estimate a common rate from total exposure.

cards.title: Binning is an analysis choice, not part of the raw observations.
cards.body: Why can fitting an exponential curve to a histogram produce estimates that depend on the bin width?
cards.answer: The histogram changes when edges and widths change, so a loss between bar heights and a curve changes too. The likelihood of raw independent waiting times uses their actual values and avoids that arbitrary binning choice. Histograms remain useful for visualization and diagnostics.
cards.takeaway: Keep visualization choices separate from the observation model.

cards.title: A flat prior is not flat in every coordinate.
cards.body: If θ has a uniform prior on (0,1), is the log-odds φ = log(θ/(1−θ)) also uniform?
cards.answer:
No. Density transforms with a Jacobian: pφ(φ) = pθ(θ(φ)) |dθ/dφ| = θ(1−θ), which depends on φ.

“Uniform” specifies a coordinate-dependent choice, not an absence of all assumptions. Bayesian inference should state the parameterization and prior.
cards.takeaway: A prior is part of the model.

cards.title: A gamma prior is conjugate to an exponential rate.
cards.body: Use a Gamma(a,b) prior on ν in shape–rate form and N independent exponential times with total T. Derive the posterior.
cards.answer: The prior kernel is ν^(a−1)e^(−bν), and the likelihood kernel is ν^N e^(−Tν). Their product is Gamma(a+N,b+T). Its mean is (a+N)/(b+T). If software uses a scale, convert it to 1/(b+T).
cards.takeaway: State shape–rate or shape–scale explicitly.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · Bayesian exponential example, pp. 61–64 · companion practice

cards.title: An improper prior can yield a proper posterior—but check it.
cards.body: With a flat prior proportional to 1 on ν>0 and N exponential observations with positive total T, what is the posterior kernel and normalized family?
cards.answer: The posterior kernel is ν^N e^(−Tν), giving Gamma(N+1,T) in shape–rate form. It is proper when T>0. The prior itself does not integrate to one, so it should not be described as a proper uniform distribution on the positive half-line.
cards.takeaway: Posterior propriety is a condition to verify.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · flat-prior exponential example · companion practice

cards.title: A credible interval answers a conditional probability question.
cards.body: What does a 95% Bayesian credible interval for θ state, and what does it depend on?
cards.answer: It contains 95% of the posterior probability under the chosen likelihood and prior, conditional on the observed data. Different interval definitions can select different sets with the same mass. Its interpretation depends on the modeling assumptions, not just on the observed counts.
cards.takeaway: Posterior uncertainty is conditional on a model.
cards.source: Lecture 06 · pp. 50–53 · transformation companion · companion practice

cards.title: Small jumps can become diffusion.
cards.body: A symmetric walk jumps left or right by Δx, each at rate 1/(2τ). How does the master equation lead to a diffusion coefficient?
cards.answer:
The incoming-minus-outgoing equation is ṗₙ=(pₙ₋₁−2pₙ+pₙ₊₁)/(2τ). Rewriting the second difference with denominator Δx² gives the continuum approximation ∂ₜp=D∂ₓₓp with D=Δx²/(2τ).

A nontrivial limit holds Δx²/τ fixed as both scales shrink.
cards.takeaway: Match the jump and time scales.

cards.title: Halving jump size requires quartering the waiting scale.
cards.body: For D=Δx²/(2τ), how must τ change if Δx is halved while D stays fixed?
cards.answer: τ must be divided by 4. The numerator becomes Δx²/4, so the denominator must shrink by the same factor. Keeping τ fixed instead would reduce D by a factor of four.
cards.takeaway: Diffusive time scales like distance squared.

cards.title: Random displacement grows like the square root of time.
cards.body: For one-dimensional diffusion with coefficient D starting at zero, what are the mean squared displacement and root-mean-square displacement?
cards.answer: E[X(t)²]=2Dt and RMS displacement=√(2Dt). Multiplying time by four doubles the RMS displacement. This differs from ballistic motion, where distance grows linearly with time.
cards.takeaway: Diffusion spreads in square-root time.

cards.title: The same rules can express different interpretations.
cards.body: Contrast a repeated-trials interpretation of probability with a Bayesian degree-of-belief interpretation.
cards.answer:
A repeated-trials interpretation ties probability to long-run frequencies under a specified repeatable process. A Bayesian interpretation uses probability to quantify uncertainty conditional on available information, including uncertainty about unknown parameters.

Both use probability rules, but what is treated as uncertain and how an inference is interpreted can differ. A prior must state the information or assumptions it represents.
cards.takeaway: Distinguish the rules from their interpretation.
